title: Hall, Yard and Docks
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. operates from a single-storey warehouse hall of 6,000 m2 in Port Sellow, Alveria. The hall provides 10 m clear height for racked and bulk storage and is joined by a small office annex for administration, dispatch and supervision.

2. The site is fully fenced. Outside the hall, a fenced yard of approximately 3,500 m2 serves all vehicle movements, manoeuvring and waiting. Access to the yard is controlled, and only scheduled carriers with an assigned door and time slot are admitted.

3. The building has 8 dock doors, all at 1.2 m dock height. Each dock door is equipped with its own dock leveller. The levellers are inspected and maintained as part of dock equipment and are only operated by trained staff.

4. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and serve Zone A receiving. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and serve Zone D dispatch. The inbound-outbound separation is fixed and no door is used in the reverse direction.

5. Every arrival is assigned in advance by the dispatcher. The dispatcher books transport, assigns a specific dock door and a time slot, and coordinates the sequence of inbound and outbound trucks per shift.

6. Drivers report on arrival and wait in the marked waiting area in the yard. Drivers do not enter the hall and do not enter the storage or picking zones. Contact with the warehouse team takes place at the dock or via the dispatcher.

7. Unloading takes place only at the assigned inbound door after documents have been presented and checked. Loading takes place only at the assigned outbound door after the dispatcher has released the load. Trucks are loaded and unloaded under supervision of the shift team.

8. The yard provides marked traffic lanes, pedestrian crossings and the driver waiting area. Pedestrian walkways inside the building are physically separated by yellow barriers. Transport discipline in the yard and in the hall is mandatory and is supervised by the shift supervisor in charge of the floor.

9. The hall houses bulk storage, picking, dispatch staging, chilled storage and services areas, supplied with electric materials-handling equipment, WMS scanners and stretch-wrapping and baling equipment. No diesel or gas-powered trucks are used inside the building.

10. The shift supervisor in charge is responsible for order and safety on the floor and in the immediate dock and yard interface during the shift. Any irregularity concerning doors, levellers, yard use or unauthorised presence is reported immediately and recorded for follow-up.

title: Zones A to F
text:
1. The 6,000 m2 hall is divided into six fixed zones, A to F. Every member of staff learns the zone layout on day one and uses zone names in all WMS transactions, handover notes and incident reports. Zone boundaries and functions do not change without authorisation from the warehouse manager.

2. Zone A — receiving (800 m2) serves inbound docks 1-4. All unloading, document checking, counting and goods inspection take place here. Nothing moves past Zone A into storage until the paperwork has been checked and the goods have been inspected and booked into the system.

3. Zone B — bulk storage (2,200 m2) holds high-bay pallet racking with 2,400 pallet positions. It is the main reserve store for packed consumer goods — food, drugstore products and household items — and feeds the pick faces in Zone C. Put-away to Zone B takes place only after goods have been booked in Zone A.

4. Within Zone B, each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg. Outside the racking, free block-stacking is permitted only up to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height. Stack height, bay load and aisle discipline are checked during the monthly racking inspection and supervised daily by the shift supervisor.

5. Zone C — picking (1,200 m2) contains ground-level pick faces and flow racks. It is the only zone where customer order picking takes place. Before each picking shift the pick faces are replenished from bulk storage in Zone B so that pickers work only against scanner tasks with available stock.

6. Zone D — dispatch (900 m2) is outbound staging in front of outbound docks 5-8. Only wrapped, labelled pallets assigned to a released outbound load are staged here. Pallets are staged by door and by load, and no unwrapped or unlabelled pallet is held in Zone D.

7. Zone E — cold zone (300 m2) is chilled storage held between +2 °C and +8 °C. It has temperature alarms and a manual temperature verification each shift. Only chilled goods are stored here, and goods requiring chill are put away to Zone E directly after inspection in Zone A.

8. Zone F — services and control (600 m2) houses value-added packing, quarantine, and returns inspection. All returns are received and inspected in Zone F, and all damaged goods held for decision are quarantined here. No quarantine stock is held in any other zone.

9. Inside Zone F is a separate ventilated hazmat cage of 60 m2. All hazardous packed goods are stored only in this cage and never elsewhere in the hall. The cage holds never more than 4,000 kg at a time, equivalent to 4 full-weight pallets.

10. Movement between zones follows the goods flow: A to B, E or F on inbound; B to C on replenishment; C to D on outbound; and inbound returns and damaged goods to F for inspection and quarantine. Staff do not move stock between zones without a WMS task, and drivers do not enter any zone and remain in the marked waiting area in the yard.

title: Shifts and Procedures
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. runs two fixed shifts, Monday to Friday: mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00. The site employs around forty people across both shifts to store and distribute packed consumer goods — food, drugstore products and household items — for about twenty regular clients.

2. There is always one shift supervisor in charge of the floor during operating hours. The shift supervisor runs the floor staff, supervises transport discipline in the hall and yard interface, and leads incident response until handover or escalation to the warehouse manager.

3. In peak season the company adds Saturday morning overtime to meet outbound demand. Overtime is exceptional and is worked only when approved in advance. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime, and no supervisor, dispatcher or operator authorises additional hours.

4. Each shift begins with task allocation and ends with a formal handover under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Pick faces in Zone C are replenished before each picking shift, cycle counts run each working day, and the cold zone temperature is manually verified each shift.

5. All warehouse work runs off fifteen written procedures, PR-01 to PR-15. The procedures are mandatory for everyone on site. If any instruction in this manual differs from the owner's brief on how the site is actually run, the brief prevails and the manual must be corrected.

6. The goods-flow procedures are PR-01 Inbound receiving, PR-02 Put-away to storage, PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces, PR-04 Order picking, PR-05 Packing and labelling, and PR-06 Outbound dispatch. They define the fixed sequence from document check in Zone A to sealed loading at docks 5-8.

7. The inventory and exception procedures are PR-07 Returns handling, PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts, and PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Returns are accepted within 14 days and inspected in Zone F, counts run daily with a signed annual stocktake, and damaged goods go to quarantine the same day they are found.

8. The safety and support procedures are PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse, PR-12 Cold-chain handling, PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response, PR-14 Emergency evacuation, and PR-15 End-of-shift handover. They cover authorisation, speed limits, protective equipment and emergency discipline.

9. Procedures are referenced by number in all training, WMS tasks and reports. Staff work only to the current version and only within their role: forklift operators drive trucks, inbound operators unload and inspect, pickers pick scanner tasks, stock controllers own counts, and dispatchers book transport and assign doors.

10. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site — operations, safety and final sign-offs — and owns the procedure system. The shift supervisors ensure the procedures are followed on every shift and review every incident report before close or escalation.

title: Management and Supervision
text:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. is led by the warehouse manager, who is the owner of the site. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site — day-to-day operations, safety, inventory accuracy and the final sign-offs. Where responsibility is delegated for a shift or a task, accountability remains with the warehouse manager.

2. The warehouse manager owns the operating framework. This includes the six-zone layout, the fifteen written procedures PR-01 to PR-15, staffing across the two shifts, and the standards for accuracy, safety and client service. No change to zones, procedures or operating hours is valid without the warehouse manager's authorisation.

3. The warehouse manager holds all final sign-offs. The manager personally signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake results and any damaged-goods write-off above 500 EUR. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime, including Saturday morning overtime in peak season, and only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators.

4. The warehouse manager is supported by 2 shift supervisors, one for the morning shift 06:00-14:00 and one for the afternoon shift 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday, plus rostered cover for approved Saturday overtime. There is always one named shift supervisor in charge of the floor during operating hours.

5. The shift supervisor in charge runs the shift. The supervisor allocates tasks to floor staff at shift start, coordinates inbound operators, pickers, forklift operators and dispatch activity through the shift, supervises discipline in the hall and at the dock and yard interface, and hands over formally to the next shift under PR-15.

6. The shift supervisor is responsible for safety and order on the floor. This includes enforcement of speed limits, aisle discipline, pedestrian separation, PPE use, dock-door discipline and correct use of materials-handling equipment. Any irregularity, near miss or breach is stopped, recorded and reported for follow-up.

7. The shift supervisor leads incident response on the shift. In case of injury, damage, spill, temperature alarm, fire alarm or evacuation, the supervisor takes charge of the floor, secures the area, directs staff and drivers, ensures roll call where required, and escalates without delay to the warehouse manager.

8. The shift supervisor exercises defined approvals within the shift. The supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to 500 EUR, approves the final disposition of inspected returns — restock, rework or scrap — on proposal from returns staff, and reviews every incident report before close or escalation.

9. The line of escalation is fixed. Floor staff report to the shift supervisor in charge. The shift supervisor reports to the warehouse manager. Dispatchers, stock controllers and the maintenance technician work within their roles but remain under the supervisor's floor authority during the shift and escalate through the supervisor unless immediate escalation to the manager is required.

10. Management presence is continuous and documented. The supervisor on duty is identified by name at shift start, is reachable on the floor throughout the shift, and records key events, counts, incidents and handover notes. The warehouse manager reviews shift records, incident reviews, inspection logs and WMS accuracy data and corrects the operation or the manual where the owner's brief requires it.

title: Operational Roles
text:
1. Floor operations are carried out by defined operational roles working under the shift supervisor in charge. Each person works only within their role and training: forklift operators, inbound operators, pickers, stock controllers, returns and packing staff, the maintenance technician, dispatchers and floaters. The roster provides about 38-40 staff in total across the two shifts.

2. Forklift operators — 8 posts — drive the company's electric materials-handling equipment. They operate the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t for general work, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t for the high bays in Zone B, and electric and hand pallet jacks for small moves. No licence, no truck: only the warehouse manager authorises new operators, and no other person permits driving.

3. Inbound operators — 6 posts — work in Zone A receiving at inbound docks 1-4. They unload only after documents have been checked, then count and inspect the goods, record quantity and visible damage, and present only inspected goods for booking into the WMS. Nothing moves past Zone A to put-away until this check is complete.

4. Pickers — 10 posts — work in Zone C picking against WMS scanner tasks. They pick only from replenished ground-level pick faces and flow racks, scan-verify every picked item before it is packed, and follow the sequence in PR-04 Order picking. Pickers do not pick from bulk storage in Zone B and do not move stock without a scanner task.

5. Stock controllers — 2 posts — own inventory accuracy day to day. They run the daily cycle counts on the rotating zone schedule, carry out the mandatory second count before any adjustment is posted, prepare recounts and adjustment proposals, and support the annual wall-to-wall stocktake. The principle that system stock is rack stock rests with them.

6. Returns and packing staff — 4 posts — work in Zone F services and control. On returns they receive goods returned within 14 days of delivery, inspect every unit, segregate quarantine stock, and propose restock, rework or scrap for approval by the shift supervisor. On packing they carry out value-added packing, labelling and operation of the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers and the cardboard baler.

7. The maintenance technician — 1 post — maintains trucks, racking and dock equipment. This includes the forklift and reach-truck fleet, pallet jacks, dock levellers at all 8 doors, racking in Zone B, and the 20 handheld WMS scanners so far as hardware is concerned. Every repair is logged, and every truck receives a documented check before its first use each day.

8. Dispatchers — 2 posts — work from the office annex and the Zone D interface. They book transport, assign each carrier a dock door and a time slot, direct drivers to the marked waiting area in the yard, stage only wrapped and labelled pallets by door and load, and release outbound loads at docks 5-8. No truck is loaded without dispatcher release.

9. Floaters — 2 posts — provide trained cover for absence across inbound, picking, packing and dispatch support. They work only to tasks they are trained for and never operate forklifts or reach trucks unless authorised as operators. Their deployment is decided by the shift supervisor at shift start and recorded in the handover.

10. All operational roles share common duties: wear high-visibility vest and class S3 safety footwear on the warehouse floor, use pedestrian walkways and crossings, keep to zone discipline and WMS scanner discipline, report damage, discrepancy or unsafe condition the same day it is found, and hand over unfinished work under PR-15. Drivers and visitors never replace these roles and never enter the hall beyond the dock.

title: Approvals and Sign-offs
text:
1. Final accountability for Harborwick 3PL Ltd. rests with the warehouse manager as owner of the site. The manager is accountable for operations, safety and inventory accuracy, holds all final sign-offs, and owns the rule that where the manual differs from the owner's brief, the brief prevails.

2. Damaged-goods write-offs are split by value at a fixed threshold of 500 EUR. The shift supervisor approves write-offs up to and including 500 EUR. Any write-off above 500 EUR is approved only by the warehouse manager, after quarantine, inspection and documentation under PR-09.

3. No damaged goods leave quarantine without a recorded approval. Goods are moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day damage is found, returns staff or stock controllers prepare the facts and value, and the authorised approver records the decision to restock, rework or scrap before any WMS adjustment.

4. Returns decisions follow the same control. Returns and packing staff in Zone F receive returns within 14 days of delivery, inspect every unit and propose restock, rework or scrap under PR-07. The final disposition of inspected returns is approved only by the shift supervisor in charge.

5. Overtime is controlled centrally. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime, including Saturday morning overtime in peak season. No shift supervisor, dispatcher, stock controller or operator authorises additional hours, and unapproved hours are not worked or paid as overtime.

6. Dock scheduling is owned by the dispatcher. The dispatcher books transport, assigns every carrier a specific door and time slot, directs drivers to the marked waiting area in the yard, and coordinates the sequence at doors 1-4 inbound only and doors 5-8 outbound only. No other role changes doors or slots.

7. Release of outbound loads is a dispatcher authority. Only wrapped, labelled pallets staged in Zone D are presented, and no truck at doors 5-8 is loaded or sealed until the dispatcher has released the load under PR-06. Inbound unloading in Zone A starts only after documents have been checked.

8. Inventory results are signed off by management. Cycle counts run every working day on a rotating zone schedule and no adjustment is ever posted without a second count under PR-08. The annual wall-to-wall stocktake is signed off personally by the warehouse manager.

9. People and equipment authorisations are reserved. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators on the rule of no licence, no truck, covering the 6 counterbalance forklifts, 4 reach trucks and pallet jacks. Every truck receives a documented check before its first use each day.

10. Incident control closes the loop. The shift supervisor in charge leads immediate response on the floor, secures the area and escalates to the warehouse manager, and reviews every incident report before close or escalation. Key approvals, counts and handovers are recorded by name and shift under PR-15.

title: Dock Booking and Arrival
text:
1. All inbound arrivals are planned in advance by the dispatcher. The dispatcher books transport with the carrier, assigns a specific inbound door from doors 1-4 and a fixed time slot, and records the booking with carrier name, trailer reference, client, expected pallet count and door. No inbound truck arrives without a booking.

2. Doors 1-4 are inbound only and serve Zone A receiving. The inbound-outbound separation is absolute: inbound trucks are never directed to doors 5-8, and outbound trucks are never directed to doors 1-4. The dispatcher coordinates the sequence across all 8 doors to avoid yard congestion and dock conflicts.

3. Time slots are set to fit the two operating shifts, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00, plus approved Saturday morning overtime in peak season. The dispatcher spaces arrivals so that Zone A has free unloading capacity, inbound operators and forklift capacity, and WMS booking capacity for each truck.

4. The carrier is informed of the door, slot, site speed limits and waiting rules at booking. On approach the driver follows yard signage, keeps to marked traffic lanes at 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h at pedestrian crossings, dock ramps and shared areas, and reports to the assigned door without blocking other doors or aisles.

5. Access to the fenced yard of 3,500 m2 is controlled. Only scheduled carriers with an assigned door and slot are admitted. Early, late or unbooked trucks wait as directed by the dispatcher and do not occupy a dock door until called forward. The shift supervisor in charge resolves conflicts on the floor and yard interface.

6. On arrival the driver reports at the dock and presents the delivery documents. Documents are checked before anything is unloaded, in line with PR-01 Inbound receiving. Unloading starts only after the check is passed and the inbound team confirms the door, leveller and Zone A space are ready.

7. Drivers wait in the marked waiting area in the yard. Drivers never enter the hall, Zone A storage areas, picking or bulk zones, and never operate warehouse equipment. All contact takes place at the dock or via the dispatcher, and drivers remain clear of forklift movements, levellers and pedestrian walkways.

8. Each dock door is at 1.2 m dock height and has its own dock leveller. Levellers are operated only by trained staff and are checked as part of dock equipment maintenance. A truck is positioned, braked and secured at the assigned door before the leveller is placed and unloading begins under supervision of the shift team.

9. The dispatcher hands each booked arrival to the shift team through the WMS and shift plan: door, slot, client goods, cold-chain or hazmat flag, and special instructions. Goods requiring chill for Zone E or hazardous packed goods for the Zone F cage are flagged at booking so that inspection and put-away capacity is ready on arrival.

10. Any deviation — missed slot, wrong trailer, damaged seals, missing papers, late arrival or door blocked — is reported immediately to the dispatcher and the shift supervisor in charge. The dispatcher re-books the door and slot, records the change, and ensures Zone A discipline is maintained: nothing moves past Zone A until paperwork is checked and goods are inspected and booked.

title: Checking and Inspection
text:
1. No unloading starts until the delivery documents have been checked in Zone A. The inbound operator compares the delivery note and transport papers against the dispatcher booking — carrier, client, purchase or inbound reference, pallet and carton count, product description, batch and expiry where shown, and any cold-chain or hazmat flag — and confirms the correct door and load.

2. If documents are missing, incomplete, or do not match the booking, the load is held at the dock. The inbound operator stops the process, informs the shift supervisor in charge and the dispatcher, and records the discrepancy. Nothing is unloaded and nothing moves past Zone A until the paperwork is resolved.

3. Once documents pass, unloading takes place at the assigned inbound door from doors 1-4 under supervision of the shift team. Only trained inbound operators and authorised forklift operators work the unloading, using electric forklifts, electric or hand pallet jacks. Drivers remain in the marked waiting area and do not enter the hall or operate equipment.

4. Goods are unloaded directly into Zone A receiving and staged by delivery for counting and inspection. Pallets are placed clear of dock levellers, pedestrian walkways and transport aisles, and cold-chain or hazmat deliveries are segregated immediately so their put-away route to Zone E or the Zone F cage stays clear.

5. Every delivery is counted in Zone A before booking. The inbound operator counts pallets and cartons or units against the checked documents, scans labels where the WMS requires it, and records overages, shortages and seal or packaging exceptions on the inbound record. Uncounted goods are never presented for booking.

6. Every delivery is inspected in Zone A before booking. The inbound operator checks outer packaging, pallet condition and stability, labelling and batch marking, visible damage, leakage, odour or contamination, and temperature indication on chilled goods. Only inspected goods are booked into the system.

7. Chilled goods flagged for Zone E are priority-checked for temperature and condition. Any doubt about the +2 °C to +8 °C range, the cold-chain evidence, or product integrity is reported at once to the shift supervisor. Such goods are not booked for put-away to Zone E until the supervisor confirms the decision under PR-12.

8. Hazardous packed goods flagged for Zone F are checked against their papers and labels without opening them. They remain segregated in Zone A under supervision until cleared for escorted put-away to the ventilated hazmat cage only. Hazmat is never put away elsewhere, and the 4,000 kg cage limit is respected at booking.

9. Damaged, suspect or non-conforming goods are separated in Zone A at the time they are found. Damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found, with the inbound record, photographs where required, and WMS quarantine status. They do not enter bulk storage in Zone B, the cold zone or the pick faces.

10. The check is closed only when documents, count and inspection agree and are recorded under PR-01. The inbound operator confirms quantity and condition in the WMS, the shift supervisor resolves any held or quarantined part of the delivery, and only booked goods are released for put-away to Zone B, E or F.

title: Booking and Release
text:
1. Only inspected goods are booked into the system. Booking takes place in Zone A after documents, count and inspection have been checked and recorded under PR-01 Inbound receiving. Goods that are uncounted, uninspected, held for paperwork, or separated as damaged are never booked as available stock.

2. Booking is a WMS transaction carried out on the handheld scanners. The inbound operator confirms client, product, quantity, pallet identity, batch and expiry where required, and storage requirement — ambient to Zone B, chilled to Zone E, hazardous packed goods to the Zone F cage, quarantine to Zone F. Each pallet booked respects the site limit of 1,000 kg including load.

3. Every booked pallet receives its system label and storage instruction before it leaves Zone A. Pallets without a WMS booking and a correct label do not move to put-away. Relabelling, over-labelling or manual movement without a scanner task is forbidden.

4. Chilled goods are booked to Zone E only when the inspection confirms cold-chain integrity for storage between +2 °C and +8 °C. The booking carries the temperature flag and priority for immediate put-away. Any load with unresolved temperature doubt is not booked to Zone E and is held for the shift supervisor decision under PR-12.

5. Hazardous packed goods are booked only to the ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F and only within its limit of 4,000 kg at a time, equivalent to 4 full-weight pallets. The booking is checked against current cage stock before release. If the new delivery would exceed the limit, the excess is not booked for put-away and remains held under supervision until space is confirmed.

6. Damaged, suspect or non-conforming goods found during checking are not booked as available. They are transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found, with WMS quarantine status, inbound reference and reason. They enter bulk storage, the cold zone or the pick faces only if inspection and approval later release them as restock.

7. Release to put-away follows booking and is given as a WMS put-away task under PR-02 Put-away to storage. Only booked goods go to put-away in Zone B, E or F. The task states destination zone, rack or location, handling equipment and priority, and staff move stock between zones only on that task.

8. Release is sequenced to keep Zone A clear and the next arrival on slot. Cold-chain pallets are released first for direct put-away to Zone E, hazmat pallets are released for escorted put-away to the cage only, and ambient pallets are released to Zone B. The shift supervisor in charge controls the order and assigns authorised forklift operators.

9. Any booking error — wrong product, quantity, batch, expiry, label or destination — stops release for that pallet. The pallet is held in Zone A, recounted and rechecked, and the booking is corrected in the WMS before a new put-away task is issued. No adjustment is posted without a second count.

10. The inbound receipt is closed only when all pallets of the delivery are accounted for as booked to storage or as held in quarantine, with documents, counts and WMS records agreeing. The inbound operator confirms completion, the shift supervisor resolves any held part, and Zone A space is released for the next booked arrival.

title: Storage Limits and Layout
text:
1. Zone B — bulk storage occupies 2,200 m2 of the 6,000 m2 hall and is the main reserve store for packed consumer goods. It holds high-bay pallet racking with 2,400 pallet positions and defined free block-stacking areas outside the racking. It feeds the pick faces in Zone C and receives only booked goods from Zone A under PR-02 Put-away to storage.

2. The governing load figure for all storage on site is 1,000 kg per pallet, load included. No pallet placed in racking or in block stack exceeds this weight. Every bay load, stack height and equipment rating in Zone B is applied on the basis of full-weight 1,000 kg pallets.

3. Each rack bay in Zone B carries at most 2,700 kg in total. The limit applies to the combined weight of all pallets, packaging and pallet timber in that bay at any time. In practice this means no more than two full-weight pallets per bay, with the remaining margin reserved for weight variation and safe handling, and never more than the bay label allows.

4. Racking is installed within the 10 m clear height of the hall and is served only by the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t for high-bay work. Counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t handle general transport to and from the end of the rack aisles but do not work inside the high bays unless the layout and task expressly permit it.

5. Free block-stacking is permitted only in marked floor areas outside the racking. In those areas stacking is limited to 3 pallets high and to 4.0 m total height including pallets and load, whichever is reached first. Any stack that would exceed 3 high or 4.0 m is split and relocated, not topped up.

6. No block stack is placed in transport aisles, rack aisles, pedestrian walkways, crossings, dock approaches, in front of emergency exits, fire equipment or the Zone E and Zone F doors. Floor markings for block areas, aisles and keep-clear zones are binding, and overhang into the aisle is treated as a breach.

7. Aisle widths in and around Zone B are fixed. Main transport aisles serving Zone B are 4.0 m wide to allow two-way electric forklift movement and safe passing. The rack storage aisles between the high bays are 3.0 m wide and are kept fully clear for reach-truck operation. Pedestrian walkways crossing or bordering Zone B are 1.2 m wide and physically separated by yellow barriers.

8. Stability and condition limits apply equally to racking and block stacks. Pallets must be sound, fully wrapped or otherwise secured, evenly loaded and within footprint. Damaged, leaning, overloaded or unstable pallets are not put away to height or to stack and are reported for quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found.

9. Zone B holds ambient packed goods only. Goods requiring chill between +2 °C and +8 °C go to Zone E, hazardous packed goods go only to the ventilated 60 m2 hazmat cage in Zone F within its 4,000 kg limit, and quarantine and returns go to Zone F. No chilled, hazmat or quarantine stock is stored in Zone B to use spare positions.

10. Limits are checked daily by the shift supervisor in charge and verified by documented inspection every month. The monthly racking inspection covers bay loads, upright and beam damage, beam levels, floor markings, aisle clearances and block-stack heights, and every repair is logged by the maintenance technician. Any overload, damage or encroachment stops put-away to that bay or floor area until cleared.

title: Put-away to Storage
text:
1. Only booked goods leave Zone A for put-away. Put-away runs under PR-02 Put-away to storage on WMS put-away tasks issued after booking under PR-01. Goods that are unbooked, held for paperwork, or separated as damaged are never moved to Zone B, Zone E or Zone F as available stock.

2. Each put-away task states client, product, quantity, pallet identity, destination zone and location, and handling priority. Staff move stock between zones only on that task, using the 20 handheld WMS scanners. Movement without a scanner task, or with a hand-written instruction, is forbidden.

3. Ambient packed goods are put away to Zone B bulk storage. Chilled goods are put away direct to Zone E cold zone, and hazardous packed goods are put away only to the ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F. Quarantine goods go to Zone F and never to Zone B or to the pick faces in Zone C.

4. Put-away is sequenced by the shift supervisor in charge to keep Zone A clear for the next booked arrival. Chilled pallets for Zone E go first without delay, hazmat pallets go by escorted move to the cage only, and ambient pallets follow to Zone B in door and booking order.

5. Put-away is carried out only by authorised forklift operators. No licence, no truck — only the warehouse manager authorises new operators. Every truck has a documented check before its first use each day, and only checked trucks are used for put-away.

6. Equipment is matched to the task and location. The 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t handle general transport from Zone A to the end of the rack aisles, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t work the high bays, and electric and hand pallet jacks handle small moves. Each pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg.

7. Placement in Zone B respects all storage limits at the moment of put-away. Each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg in total, so no more than two full-weight pallets are placed in one bay. Free block-stacking is limited to marked floor areas only, up to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height, whichever is reached first.

8. Discipline on the route and at the location is mandatory. Operators keep to main transport aisles of 4.0 m and rack aisles of 3.0 m, keep 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers fully clear, and observe 10 km/h inside the building and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps. Overhang, aisle parking and blocking of emergency exits or fire equipment stop put-away until cleared.

9. Every pallet is scan-confirmed at its storage location. The operator scans the pallet label and the location label, confirms upright and beam condition before placing to height, and reports any damaged, leaning, overloaded or unstable pallet, rack damage or wrong-location stock at once. Such pallets are not put away to height and damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found.

10. Put-away is closed in the WMS when all booked pallets of the delivery are confirmed in Zone B, E or F, or as held in quarantine, with records agreeing. Any booking error or misplaced pallet is held, recounted and rechecked, and corrected before a new task is issued. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count, and incomplete put-away is handed over by name under PR-15.

title: Racking Inspections
text:
1. All high-bay racking in Zone B receives a documented safety inspection every calendar month. The inspection is planned in advance so that every rack bay, beam level and aisle in the 2,200 m2 bulk store with its 2,400 pallet positions is checked, and no bay is carried forward unchecked to the next month.

2. The monthly inspection is carried out by the maintenance technician together with the shift supervisor in charge, with Zone B kept in operation under traffic control. Results are recorded bay by bay in the racking log, signed by name and date, and every repair found is logged for follow-up. The warehouse manager reviews the log and orders correction where needed.

3. Each rack bay is checked against its limit of 2,700 kg total. The inspector verifies pallet count per bay, the 1,000 kg per pallet governing weight, bay load labels, and any sign of overloading. Any bay found above 2,700 kg is stopped for put-away immediately, unloaded to a compliant load, and reported to the shift supervisor.

4. Uprights, beams, bracing, base plates and floor fixings are checked for impact damage, bending, cracking, missing pins or clips, and corrosion. Beam levels are checked for correct engagement and horizontal position within the 10 m clear height. Damaged components are red-tagged, offloaded if unsafe, and quarantined from use until repaired.

5. Free block-stacking areas outside the racking are checked in the same inspection. Stacks are limited to marked floor areas only, to 3 pallets high and 4.0 m total height including pallets and load, whichever is reached first. Overheight, overhanging or unstable stacks are split and rebuilt the same day they are found.

6. Aisles, markings and clearances form part of every inspection. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m and rack storage aisles of 3.0 m must be fully clear and markings legible. Pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers, crossings, emergency exits, fire equipment and the doors to Zone E and Zone F must be unobstructed.

7. Pallet and load condition in the racks is inspected for sound pallets, secure wrapping, even loading and placement within footprint. Damaged, leaning, overloaded or unstable pallets are not left at height. They are lowered by an authorised operator on a checked truck and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found.

8. Equipment interface is verified during the inspection. Only the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t work the high bays, with the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t delivering to the aisle ends. Aisle damage patterns, wheel marks and repeated impacts are recorded as evidence of driving discipline and followed up under PR-10.

9. Any damage, overload or encroachment that threatens safety triggers immediate action. The shift supervisor stops put-away and picking access to that bay or floor area, secures it with barriers or tape, informs the warehouse manager, and assigns only authorised operators to make it safe. Work resumes only after clearance is recorded.

10. The inspection is closed only when all findings have a disposition. Minor tightening and relabelling are completed and signed off, damaged parts are ordered and replaced by or under the maintenance technician with every repair logged, and WMS locations for blocked bays remain suspended until release. Incomplete items are handed over by name under PR-15 and carried into the next shift plan.

title: Cold Zone Handling
text:
1. Zone E — cold zone is a fixed 300 m2 chilled store inside the 6,000 m2 hall. It holds only goods requiring chill and no other stock. Ambient packed goods remain in Zone B, hazardous packed goods remain in the ventilated cage in Zone F, and quarantine stock remains in Zone F outside the cold zone.

2. The storage condition in Zone E is held between +2 °C and +8 °C at all times. The range applies to every position in the zone, on every shift, Monday to Friday and during any approved Saturday morning overtime. No product requiring chill is stored, staged or left in any other zone to use spare capacity.

3. All cold-chain work runs under PR-12 Cold-chain handling. chilled deliveries are flagged by the dispatcher at booking, priority-checked in Zone A for temperature and condition, booked to Zone E only when integrity is confirmed, and put away direct to Zone E without delay. Any unresolved temperature doubt stops booking to Zone E for supervisor decision.

4. Temperature in Zone E is monitored by fixed alarms plus a manual verification each shift. The shift supervisor in charge ensures the manual check is carried out on both shifts, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, with the measured value, time, name and any alarm condition recorded. The record is handed over under PR-15 and reviewed by the warehouse manager.

5. If the temperature reaches or passes outside +2 °C to +8 °C, or an alarm activates, the shift supervisor takes charge. The supervisor secures the zone, checks doors and equipment, segregates affected stock on the WMS, informs the warehouse manager, and holds all put-away, replenishment and dispatch of chilled goods until clearance is recorded. Affected goods are not picked or dispatched without approval.

6. Door and dwell discipline keeps the condition stable. Zone E doors are kept closed except for immediate put-away, count or replenishment moves, and pallets are not staged in the doorway, in transport aisles or in Zone A longer than needed. Forklift operators minimise time outside the zone and return chilled pallets to temperature immediately after scan confirmation.

7. Put-away and movements in Zone E use only authorised operators on checked electric trucks. Each pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg. Floor markings, aisle widths and pedestrian separation apply as elsewhere: 4.0 m main aisles, 3.0 m storage aisles where applicable, 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers, 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones and ramps.

8. Stock accuracy in Zone E follows the same controls as the rest of the site. Counts are carried out on the daily rotating schedule with minimal door-open time, no adjustment is ever posted without a second count, and damaged, leaking or temperature-suspect goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found. Quarantine goods are never held inside Zone E after discovery.

9. Hygiene and segregation are mandatory. Packaging must be intact, clean and within footprint, spillages or odour are reported at once and cleaned under supervision, and batch and expiry marking is verified at booking and at count. Cold-chain evidence from inbound — temperature indication, logger data where provided — is kept with the inbound record.

10. The maintenance technician maintains the refrigeration plant, door seals, alarms and temperature displays, and logs every repair. Any fault, alarm failure, door defect or missed manual verification is reported immediately to the shift supervisor and the warehouse manager, stops routine chilled put-away until made safe, and is carried by name in the handover until closed.

title: Hazmat Cage Limits
text:
1. The only place where hazardous packed goods may be held is the separate ventilated hazmat cage inside Zone F services and control. The cage has a fixed floor area of 60 m2, is physically separated from packing, quarantine and returns inspection, and is marked and kept locked except for authorised moves.

2. Hazmat never sits anywhere else in the hall or yard. It is not stored in Zone B bulk storage, Zone C picking, Zone D dispatch, Zone E cold zone, Zone A receiving except for segregated checking on arrival, or in any other part of Zone F. Any pallet found outside the cage is treated as a breach and moved back under supervision the same day.

3. The cage holds never more than 4,000 kg of hazardous goods at a time. The limit applies to the combined weight of goods, packaging and pallets inside the cage at any moment, on every shift, including peak season and Saturday overtime. No new booking is released for put-away if it would exceed the limit.

4. The governing pallet weight of 1,000 kg, load included, applies in full. At most 4 full-weight pallets may be in the cage at one time. Lighter pallets do not create extra places: the kilogram limit and the 4-pallet equivalent together cap quantity, and the shift supervisor stops intake when either is reached.

5. All hazmat work runs under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. Deliveries are flagged by the dispatcher at booking, checked in Zone A against papers and labels without opening, booked only to the cage within the 4,000 kg limit, and put away by escorted move only. Returns containing hazmat are received and inspected in Zone F and go only to the cage or to quarantine as decided.

6. Put-away and removal use only authorised forklift operators on checked electric trucks, with a second person escorting where PR-13 requires it. Each move is a WMS task stating cage location and priority. Pallets are scan-confirmed at the cage location, placed within footprint, stable and labelled, and never double-stacked unless the cage layout expressly permits it.

7. Separation inside Zone F is mandatory. The cage is kept clear of packing materials, cardboard baler output, quarantine pallets, returns staging and general storage. A keep-clear zone at the cage door is maintained for access, ventilation and spill response, and no pallet is staged in the doorway, in transport aisles or across the 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers.

8. Spill, leak, odour, damaged packaging or unreadable hazard labelling stops all work at the cage. The operator stops the truck, leaves the immediate area safe, alerts the shift supervisor in charge, and no further put-away or picking of hazmat takes place until the supervisor has assessed, segregated affected stock and ordered clean-up under PR-13 with damage quarantine in Zone F the same day.

9. Quantity is checked before every move and verified daily. The shift supervisor confirms current cage stock against the 4,000 kg limit before releasing inbound put-away, and stock controllers include the cage in the daily rotating cycle counts with no adjustment posted without a second count. Any excess, miscount or unlabelled pallet is held, recounted and reported to the warehouse manager.

10. The maintenance technician maintains cage ventilation, lighting, racking, signage, fire and spill equipment and logs every repair, and the shift supervisor ensures manual checks, WMS records and handover notes under PR-15 record quantity, condition and incidents by name. Faults, alarms or breaches stop hazmat intake until cleared, with final disposition of damaged hazmat approved only under the 500 EUR write-off rule.

title: Replenishment of Pick Faces
text:
1. Pick faces in Zone C are replenished from bulk storage in Zone B before each picking shift, under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Morning picking starting 06:00 and afternoon picking starting 14:00 both begin only with replenished faces. Pickers work only against scanner tasks with available stock.

2. Replenishment is a WMS task, not a manual decision. The system generates replenishment demand from outbound orders, minimum levels and empty pick locations, and the shift supervisor in charge sequences it in the shift plan. Staff do not move stock from Zone B to Zone C without a scanner task on the 20 handheld WMS scanners.

3. Only booked, available stock is used for replenishment. Goods held for paperwork in Zone A, quarantine stock in Zone F, hazmat in the Zone F cage and any pallet with unresolved count, damage or booking error are never sent to the pick faces. Unbooked movement to Zone C is forbidden.

4. The shift supervisor assigns replenishment moves at shift start to authorised forklift operators only. No licence, no truck — only the warehouse manager authorises operators. Every truck has a documented check before its first use each day, and only checked electric trucks are used.

5. Equipment is matched to the move. The 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t pull reserve pallets from the high bays in Zone B, the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t carry out general transport to Zone C, and electric and hand pallet jacks handle small top-ups. Each pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg.

6. The route follows fixed discipline. Operators keep to main transport aisles of 4.0 m and rack aisles of 3.0 m, keep 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers fully clear, and observe 10 km/h inside the building and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps. Aisles, exits and fire equipment are never blocked for staging.

7. At the bulk location the operator scan-confirms pallet and location, checks pallet stability, wrapping and bay condition, and reports any damaged, leaning or overloaded pallet at once. Such pallets are not sent to picking and damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found.

8. At the pick face in Zone C the operator scan-confirms the destination location, places full pallets or replenishes flow-rack lanes to the defined fill level without overfilling, and confirms the move in the WMS. Overstock above the face capacity is returned to its Zone B location, not left in aisles or in Zone C gangways.

9. Replenishment is completed before picking starts, with urgent top-ups during the shift only on new WMS tasks. The shift supervisor monitors completion, resolves shortages by substituting locations or re-prioritising picks, and ensures no picker is sent to an empty or unconfirmed face.

10. The replenishment is closed in the WMS when all tasks for the shift are confirmed, with any exception — short bulk location, damaged stock, wrong location or scanner error — recounted, rechecked and handed over by name under PR-15. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count, and incomplete faces are flagged to stock controllers for the daily cycle count.

title: Scanner Order Picking
text:
1. All customer order picking takes place only in Zone C picking, on ground-level pick faces and flow racks, under PR-04 Order picking. Pickers work only against WMS scanner tasks on the handheld scanners and never pick from bulk storage in Zone B, from quarantine in Zone F, or without a task.

2. Picking starts only after the faces for the shift have been replenished from Zone B under PR-03. The morning shift from 06:00 and the afternoon shift from 14:00 pick from confirmed, available faces. The shift supervisor in charge sequences tasks and does not send pickers to empty or unconfirmed locations.

3. Picking is carried out by trained pickers — 10 posts — under the shift supervisor in charge. Floaters cover picking only when trained for it. Forklift operators supply full pallets to the faces; pickers work on foot or with hand and electric pallet jacks for small moves and never operate forklifts or reach trucks unless authorised.

4. Each task states client, order, product, quantity, batch and expiry where required, pick location in Zone C, and destination for packing and Zone D. The picker follows the scanner sequence location by location, confirms the location label first, then picks the stated quantity.

5. Every picked item is scan-verified before it is packed. The picker scans the product or carton label and the pick-face label as the WMS requires, checks quantity, description, batch and expiry on the scanner screen, and only then confirms the pick. Any scan mismatch stops that pick until resolved.

6. Shortages, wrong stock, damaged packaging, unreadable labels or expiry and batch doubts are reported at once in Zone C. The location is flagged in the WMS, the goods are not packed as good stock, and damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found. No adjustment is posted without a second count by stock controllers.

7. Picked goods are placed cleanly on pallets or into cartons without overhang, overheight or mixing of orders, batches or clients unless the task expressly requires it. Each pallet, load included, respects the site limit of 1,000 kg. Unstable, leaning or damaged pallets are rebuilt or segregated before onward movement.

8. After scan verification the goods pass to packing and labelling under PR-05. Pickers ensure each unit, carton or pallet carries the correct order and handling identity so that only labelled pallets move to Zone D. Unlabelled or unverified pallets are never staged for dispatch.

9. Discipline in Zone C is mandatory throughout picking. Pedestrian walkways of 1.2 m behind yellow barriers are used for all foot movement, main aisles of 4.0 m and rack aisles of 3.0 m are kept clear, and pallet jacks give way at crossings and pedestrian zones at 5 km/h. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear are worn at all times.

10. Tasks are closed in the WMS only when every pick is scan-confirmed or flagged as an exception, with quantities, batches and labels agreeing. Incomplete orders, short faces and scanner errors are handed over by name under PR-15, faces needing top-up are returned to the replenishment queue, and verified picks are released for transfer to Zone D under PR-05 and PR-06.

title: Transfer to Dispatch
text:
1. Only scan-verified picks leave Zone C for dispatch. Transfer to Zone D takes place under PR-05 Packing and labelling and PR-06 Outbound dispatch, after every item has been scan-verified in Zone C and packed against the WMS task. Unverified, unlabelled or exception-flagged goods are never moved to Zone D.

2. Each transfer carries its WMS identity. The pallet or carton shows client, order, destination, quantity and batch and expiry where required, confirmed on the handheld scanners. Pallets without a correct label and system booking do not enter Zone D and are held in Zone C for correction.

3. Movement from Zone C to Zone D is a WMS task on the 20 handheld scanners. Staff move stock between zones only on that task. Hand-written instructions, manual carries without a scan, and mixing of orders, batches or clients on one pallet unless the task expressly requires it are forbidden.

4. Packing and labelling are completed before staging. Goods are packed cleanly without overhang, labelled, and then stretch-wrapped on the 2 semi-automatic wrappers in Zone D or the packing area. Only wrapped, labelled pallets assigned to a released outbound load are staged in Zone D in front of docks 5-8.

5. Each pallet, load included, respects the site limit of 1,000 kg. Overweight, leaning, unstable or damaged pallets are rebuilt or segregated before transfer. Damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found and never enter Zone D as good stock.

6. Transfer is carried out by trained pickers with hand and electric pallet jacks for small moves and by authorised forklift operators for full-pallet moves. No licence, no truck — only the warehouse manager authorises operators. Every truck has a documented check before its first use each day.

7. Route discipline is mandatory. Operators keep to main transport aisles of 4.0 m, keep 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers fully clear, and observe 10 km/h inside the building and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps. Aisles, emergency exits, fire equipment and dock approaches are never blocked for staging.

8. In Zone D pallets are staged strictly by door and by load as directed by the dispatcher. The dispatcher books transport, assigns doors 5-8 outbound only with time slots, and releases each load under PR-06. No truck is loaded or sealed until the dispatcher has released the load.

9. The shift supervisor in charge sequences the flow to keep picking, packing and staging balanced. Cold-chain pallets for immediate dispatch are prioritised without breaking temperature discipline, hazmat moves remain only under PR-13 where permitted, and incomplete orders wait in Zone C and are not staged as complete loads.

10. Transfer is closed in the WMS when every verified pick is confirmed as packed, labelled, wrapped and staged to its door and load, or flagged as an exception. Shortages, mispicks, label errors and scanner faults are recounted and rechecked with no adjustment posted without a second count, and unfinished staging is handed over by name under PR-15.

title: Packing and Wrapping
text:
1. Only scan-verified picks are packed and wrapped for outbound. Packing runs under PR-05 Packing and labelling after every item has been scan-verified in Zone C. Unverified, unlabelled or exception-flagged goods are never packed as good stock and never enter Zone D.

2. Packing is a WMS task on the 20 handheld scanners. Each task states client, order, product, quantity, batch and expiry where required, and destination load and door. Staff pack and label only to that task, and manual packing without a scanner task is forbidden.

3. Packing is carried out by trained pickers and the 4 returns and packing staff under the shift supervisor in charge. Value-added packing takes place in the packing areas in Zone F and at the Zone C to Zone D interface. Floaters cover packing only when trained for it.

4. Goods are packed cleanly by order, batch and client as the task requires. Cartons are closed, sealed and squared, units are placed without overhang, crushing or mixing unless the task expressly requires it, and expiry and batch marking is checked against the scanner. Damaged packaging is segregated at once.

5. Every carton, unit and pallet receives its correct outbound identity before it leaves packing. Labels show client, order, destination, quantity and batch and expiry where required, confirmed by scan. Pallets without a correct label and system booking do not move to wrapping or to Zone D.

6. Each pallet, load included, respects the site limit of 1,000 kg. Pallets must be sound, evenly loaded, within footprint and stable before wrapping. Overweight, leaning, unstable or damaged pallets are rebuilt or segregated, and damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found.

7. All outbound pallets are stretch-wrapped on the 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers. Wrapping is full, tight and anchored to the pallet base, covering to a stable height without loose tails or dragging film. Unwrapped or poorly wrapped pallets are re-wrapped and are never staged in Zone D.

8. Cardboard waste, damaged cartons and backing from packing are removed immediately and fed to the cardboard baler. Packing benches, wrappers and the transfer route to Zone D are kept clear, with main aisles of 4.0 m and 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers unobstructed and 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones observed.

9. Wrapped, labelled pallets are confirmed in the WMS as packed and released for transfer to Zone D staging by door and load. Chilled goods are packed and moved without delay to protect the +2 °C to +8 °C chain, and hazmat moves remain only under PR-13. No truck at doors 5-8 is loaded until the dispatcher releases the load under PR-06.

10. Packing is closed only when every verified pick is confirmed as packed, labelled and wrapped or flagged as an exception. Label errors, short quantities, wrapper faults and scanner faults are recounted and rechecked with no adjustment posted without a second count, and unfinished packing is handed over by name under PR-15 with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Staging and Loading
text:
1. Zone D — dispatch is outbound staging of 900 m2 in front of outbound docks 5-8. Only wrapped, labelled pallets assigned to a released outbound load are staged here, placed strictly by door and by load. Unwrapped, unlabelled or unassigned pallets are never held in Zone D.

2. Staging is a WMS task under PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Each pallet is confirmed on the handheld scanners as packed, wrapped and labelled, with client, order, destination, quantity and batch and expiry where required, and directed to its door and load. Movement without a scanner task is forbidden.

3. The dispatcher owns staging order and door allocation. The dispatcher books transport, assigns each carrier a specific door from doors 5-8 and a time slot, and records trailer reference, client, pallet count and load. Doors 5-8 are outbound only and are never used for inbound.

4. No truck at doors 5-8 is loaded or sealed until the dispatcher has released the load. Release confirms that all pallets for the load are wrapped, labelled, staged and system-allocated, with cold-chain and hazmat flags cleared. Early or partial loading before release is forbidden.

5. On arrival the driver reports to the assigned door and waits in the marked waiting area in the yard. Drivers do not enter the hall or Zone D, do not operate forklifts, pallet jacks or levellers, and remain clear of staging, wrapping and forklift movements. Contact is at the dock or via the dispatcher.

6. Loading takes place only at the assigned outbound door at 1.2 m dock height. The truck is positioned, braked and secured before the dock leveller is placed by trained staff. Each of the 8 doors has its own leveller, maintained as dock equipment and logged by the maintenance technician.

7. Loading is carried out by authorised forklift operators and trained dispatch support under the shift supervisor in charge. No licence, no truck — only the warehouse manager authorises operators. Every truck has a documented check before its first use each day, and each pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg.

8. Pallets are loaded in load sequence, stable, squared and within footprint, without overhang or damage to wrapping and labels. The team counts and scan-confirms each pallet onto the trailer against the released load, and any shortage, damage, label error or overweight pallet stops that load until resolved. Damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day.

9. Route and dock discipline are mandatory throughout. Operators keep to main aisles of 4.0 m, keep 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers fully clear, and observe 10 km/h inside the building, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and dock ramps. Dock approaches, exits and fire equipment are never blocked.

10. The load is closed only when WMS, staging and trailer agree. The dispatcher confirms completion, the trailer is sealed and the seal number recorded, and documents are handed to the driver at the dock. Incomplete loads, reseals or door changes are recorded and handed over by name under PR-15, with vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Load and Capacity Rules
text:
1. The governing load figure for all outbound planning is 1,000 kg per pallet, load included. No pallet presented for staging, loading or dispatch exceeds this weight. Every trailer load, van load and per-shift promise is calculated on the basis of full-weight 1,000 kg pallets.

2. Contracted curtain-side trailers are rated at 24,000 kg on 33 floor positions. Weight is the limiting factor: 24,000 kg divided by 1,000 kg allows 24 full-weight pallets per trailer, even though 33 floor positions are physically available. No trailer is loaded beyond 24,000 kg or beyond 24 full-weight pallets.

3. Lighter pallets do not create extra weight allowance. A trailer may use additional floor positions up to 33 only when the total weight remains within 24,000 kg and every pallet remains stable, squared and within footprint. The dispatcher checks weight and positions together before release under PR-06.

4. The delivery van is rated at 1,200 kg on 6 positions. It carries one full-weight 1,000 kg pallet only, with the remaining 200 kg reserved for packaging variation and safe securing. Any consignment heavier than one full-weight pallet, or requiring more than the van rating, goes by trailer and is never split to overload the van.

5. Van loading respects stability as well as weight. Pallets for the van must be sound, wrapped on the 2 semi-automatic wrappers, labelled and secured before departure. Loose cartons, overhang or stacking above safe height in the van are forbidden, and overweight or unstable pallets are rebuilt or moved to trailer dispatch.

6. Outbound throughput is capped by dock capacity. Zone D serves 4 outbound doors, doors 5-8, each handling at most 3 trailer loads per shift. This fixed rate sets the maximum promise to clients at 288 full-weight pallets per shift: 4 doors multiplied by 3 loads multiplied by 24 pallets.

7. The 288-pallet figure applies to the two rostered shifts, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00, and to any approved Saturday morning overtime in peak season. No dispatcher, supervisor or client commitment exceeds this limit, and only the warehouse manager approves overtime to add capacity.

8. The dispatcher owns load and capacity discipline. The dispatcher books transport to trailer or van by weight and positions, assigns doors 5-8 with time slots, sequences the 3 loads per door per shift, and releases no load until WMS weight, pallet count and staging by door and load agree.

9. Hazmat consignments remain within the cage limit at dispatch. The ventilated 60 m2 cage in Zone F holds never more than 4,000 kg at a time, equivalent to 4 full-weight pallets. Outbound staging in Zone D never bypasses this cap, and all hazmat moves run only under PR-13 with escorted handling.

10. Any load that would exceed pallet, trailer, van or shift limits is stopped before loading. The shift supervisor in charge holds the excess in Zone D or Zone C, informs the dispatcher and records the exception, and the load is replanned to the next slot or trailer. Incomplete loads are handed over by name under PR-15 with no adjustment posted without a second count.

title: Daily Cycle Counts
text:
1. Cycle counts run every working day, Monday to Friday, on a rotating zone schedule under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. The schedule covers all storage locations in turn — Zone B bulk storage with its 2,400 pallet positions, Zone C pick faces, Zone E cold zone, Zone D staging and Zone F including quarantine and the ventilated hazmat cage — so that system stock is verified against rack stock continuously.

2. Stock controllers — 2 posts — own the count programme day to day. They prepare the daily count list from the WMS, sequence locations with the shift supervisor in charge, carry out counts with the 20 handheld scanners, and ensure results, recounts and adjustment proposals are recorded by name, date and shift.

3. Counts are carried out without stopping the flow. The shift supervisor balances counting, replenishment from Zone B to Zone C, put-away from Zone A and staging to Zone D, and assigns traffic control where counters and forklifts work the same aisle. Main aisles of 4.0 m, rack aisles of 3.0 m and 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers stay clear.

4. Each count task states zone, aisle, bay or location, product, batch and expiry where required, and system quantity. The counter scans the location label then the pallet or product label, counts pallets, cartons and units as the task requires, and confirms the result in the WMS. Counting without a scanner task or from memory is forbidden.

5. No adjustment is ever posted on a first count alone. Every difference between system and floor — overage, shortage, wrong product, wrong batch or expiry, damaged or unlabelled pallet — triggers a mandatory second count by a different person, normally the second stock controller or the shift supervisor, before any correction is proposed.

6. Zone E is counted with minimal door-open time to protect the +2 °C to +8 °C range. Counts are batched, doors are kept closed except for immediate access, and temperature alarms and the manual verification each shift continue in parallel. Temperature-suspect, leaking or damaged goods found during the count go to quarantine in Zone F the same day.

7. The hazmat cage in Zone F is counted in place under PR-13. Counters check quantity against the 4,000 kg limit, equivalent to 4 full-weight pallets, verify labels and condition without opening packs, and stop on any leak, odour or damaged packaging for supervisor assessment. No hazmat pallet is moved for counting outside the cage.

8. Damaged, suspect or non-conforming stock found during any count is segregated at once. It is flagged in the WMS, transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found, and excluded from available stock for replenishment and picking. Block-stacked pallets above 3 high or 4.0 m, unstable or overweight pallets above 1,000 kg, and any rack bay above 2,700 kg are reported to the supervisor immediately.

9. Count results are closed daily in the WMS. Matched locations are confirmed, differences with a completed second count are proposed for adjustment with reason, evidence and count names, and unresolved locations are recounted and carried forward. Adjustments follow the approval rule and the annual stocktake is signed off personally by the warehouse manager.

10. Daily counts are handed over under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Unfinished zones, second counts outstanding, quarantine moves and scanner faults are recorded by name for the next shift, with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout and 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones observed. The warehouse manager reviews accuracy data and corrects the operation where the brief requires it.

title: Annual Stocktake
text:
1. The site shuts down once a year for a full wall-to-wall stocktake under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. All storage locations are counted in one exercise — Zone B bulk storage with its 2,400 pallet positions, Zone C pick faces and flow racks, Zone E cold zone, Zone D staging, and Zone F including value-added packing, quarantine, returns and the ventilated hazmat cage — with no zone omitted or sampled.

2. The stocktake is planned and ordered by the warehouse manager as owner of the site. The manager sets the date, freezes inbound, put-away, replenishment, picking and dispatch for the count window, suspends dock bookings at doors 1-4 and 5-8, and ensures both shifts and any peak-season Saturday overtime are covered by the plan.

3. Preparation is owned by the 2 stock controllers with the shift supervisors. They tidy and square all pallets, confirm bay and location labels are legible, clear Zone A receiving of unbooked goods, isolate quarantine stock in Zone F, verify the hazmat cage quantity against its 4,000 kg limit, and preload count tasks onto the 20 handheld WMS scanners.

4. Counting is carried out by paired teams under supervisor control. Each team comprises a counter and a checker from different roles — stock controllers, inbound operators, pickers, returns and packing staff and floaters — so that no location is counted and confirmed by the same person. The supervisor in charge assigns aisles and records attendance by name.

5. Every location is counted on the scanner against system quantity. The team scans the location label then the pallet or product label, counts pallets, cartons and units with batch and expiry where required, and confirms or flags the result in the WMS. Counting from memory, on paper alone, or without a scanner task is forbidden.

6. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Every difference — overage, shortage, wrong product, wrong batch or expiry, damaged or unlabelled pallet — is immediately recounted by a second team, normally led by a stock controller or the shift supervisor, before any correction is proposed with reason and evidence.

7. Zone E is counted with minimum door-open time to hold +2 °C to +8 °C. Doors stay closed except for immediate access, alarms and manual verification continue, and temperature-suspect, leaking or damaged goods go to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found and are excluded from available stock.

8. The hazmat cage is counted in place under PR-13. Teams verify weight against the 4,000 kg cap, equivalent to 4 full-weight 1,000 kg pallets, and check labels and packaging without opening packs. Any leak, odour, damage or excess stops the count at the cage for supervisor assessment and report to the warehouse manager.

9. Storage limits found during the stocktake are enforced at once. Any rack bay above 2,700 kg, block stack above 3 pallets high or 4.0 m, pallet above 1,000 kg, or unstable or damaged pallet is reported to the supervisor, lowered or rebuilt by an authorised operator on a checked truck, and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day where required.

10. The stocktake is closed only by personal sign-off of the warehouse manager. The manager reviews all first and second counts, quarantine moves, recounts outstanding and adjustment proposals, approves write-offs above 500 EUR with the supervisor approving up to 500 EUR, signs the results by name and date, and orders any manual correction where the brief requires it. Incomplete items are handed over by name under PR-15.

title: Recounts and Adjustments
text:
1. No WMS adjustment is ever posted on a first count alone. Every difference found in a daily cycle count or the annual wall-to-wall stocktake — overage, shortage, wrong product, wrong batch or expiry, wrong location, damaged or unlabelled pallet — triggers a mandatory recount before any correction is proposed under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts.

2. The recount is carried out by a different person from the first counter. Normally the second stock controller or the shift supervisor in charge recounts, using a fresh WMS task on the handheld scanners. No location is counted and confirmed by the same person, and counting from memory or without a scanner task is forbidden.

3. Both counts are recorded by name, date and shift with location label, pallet identity, product, quantity, batch and expiry where required, and system quantity. The counter scans the location then the pallet or product label, counts pallets, cartons and units as tasked, and confirms the result. Photographs and inbound references are added where damage or mislabelling is involved.

4. If first and second counts agree, the result is proposed for adjustment with reason and evidence. If they disagree, a third check is ordered by the shift supervisor, normally with the supervisor present in the aisle. Unresolved locations remain suspended for replenishment and picking and are carried forward, not force-adjusted to system.

5. Stock controllers — 2 posts — own recounts and adjustment proposals day to day. They prepare the recount list, sequence it with the shift supervisor to avoid blocking put-away from Zone A, replenishment from Zone B to Zone C and staging to Zone D, and ensure traffic control where counters and forklifts share 4.0 m main aisles and 3.0 m rack aisles.

6. Damaged, suspect or non-conforming stock found during any recount is excluded from adjustment as available stock. It is flagged in the WMS and transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found. It re-enters bulk storage, the cold zone or the pick faces only if inspection and approval later release it as restock.

7. Value control applies before posting. Adjustments that write off damaged goods are approved up to and including 500 EUR by the shift supervisor in charge, and above 500 EUR only by the warehouse manager under PR-09. No damaged goods leave quarantine without that recorded approval, and the annual stocktake results are signed personally by the warehouse manager.

8. Zone E and hazmat recounts follow special discipline. Zone E is recounted with minimal door-open time to hold +2 °C to +8 °C, with alarms and manual verification each shift continuing. The ventilated hazmat cage in Zone F is recounted in place under PR-13 without opening packs, checked against its 4,000 kg limit, equivalent to 4 full-weight 1,000 kg pallets, with any leak, odour or damage stopping work for supervisor assessment.

9. Posting is a WMS transaction only after recount and approval agree. The authorised approver confirms quantity, value, reason and disposition — correct location balance, restock, rework or scrap — and the adjustment is posted by the stock controller or supervisor. Wrong postings are reversed only by a new recounted correction, never by manual overwrite.

10. Every recount and adjustment is closed and handed over under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Matched locations are confirmed, posted adjustments, quarantine moves, outstanding recounts and scanner faults are recorded by name for the next shift, with vests and class S3 footwear worn and 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones observed. The warehouse manager reviews accuracy data and corrects the operation where the brief requires it.

title: Returns Inspection
text:
1. All customer returns are received and inspected only in Zone F services and control, under PR-07 Returns handling. No return is accepted in Zone A receiving, Zone C picking or Zone D dispatch, and no returned pallet is placed direct to bulk storage, the cold zone or the pick faces before inspection.

2. Returns are accepted only within 14 days of delivery to the customer. Returns staff check the delivery date, return note and WMS order reference on the handheld scanners at receipt. Goods outside the 14-day window are refused and the refusal is recorded with reason, date and name for the dispatcher and the shift supervisor.

3. Returns arrive by booked transport and are directed by the dispatcher to an assigned door and slot. Drivers wait in the marked waiting area in the yard and do not enter Zone F. Returns are unloaded by trained staff with hand or electric pallet jacks and moved to the returns inspection area in Zone F on a WMS task.

4. Every returned unit is inspected, without sampling. The 4 returns and packing staff check quantity, product identity, outer packaging, seal integrity, labelling, batch and expiry where required, visible damage, leakage, odour and contamination, and for chilled goods temperature indication. No unit is passed as good stock without this individual check.

5. Returned chilled goods are segregated immediately and checked first. They do not re-enter Zone E at +2 °C to +8 °C until integrity is confirmed under PR-12. Any temperature doubt, broken seal or damaged insulation is reported to the shift supervisor in charge and the goods are held separately pending decision.

6. Returned hazardous packed goods are checked against papers and labels without opening them. They remain segregated under supervision and go only to the ventilated 60 m2 hazmat cage within its 4,000 kg limit, or to quarantine, as PR-13 requires. They are never mixed with general returns or packing materials.

7. Results are recorded by unit in the WMS on the 20 handheld scanners. Staff scan the return label and location, confirm client, order, product, quantity, batch and expiry, photograph damage where required, and flag each unit as pending restock, rework or scrap proposal. Inspection without a scanner task is forbidden.

8. Goods found damaged, soiled, leaking, temperature-suspect or non-conforming during inspection are segregated at once. They are flagged in the WMS and transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found. They are excluded from available stock for replenishment and picking until a formal disposition is approved.

9. Returns staff propose the disposition for every inspected unit — restock, rework or scrap — but do not decide it. The proposal with evidence and quantity is presented to the shift supervisor in charge, who approves the final disposition of inspected returns. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count by stock controllers.

10. The inspection is closed only when all units of the return are accounted for as inspected and recorded as awaiting disposition, in quarantine, or released by approval. Incomplete inspections, held chilled or hazmat units and scanner faults are handed over by name under PR-15, with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn and 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones observed.

title: Disposition Decisions
text:
1. Every inspected return receives a formal disposition decision — restock, rework or scrap — under PR-07 Returns handling. No returned unit re-enters bulk storage, the cold zone or the pick faces, and no WMS adjustment is posted, until that decision has been proposed, approved and recorded.

2. Returns and packing staff — 4 posts — prepare the proposal in Zone F. After inspecting every unit, they flag each unit in the WMS on the handheld scanners as proposed restock, proposed rework or proposed scrap, with quantity, product, batch and expiry where required, photographs where damage applies, and reason. Proposal is not approval.
