3. Restock is proposed only for clean, intact, fully labelled goods within date, with seal integrity and, for chilled goods, confirmed +2 °C to +8 °C integrity under PR-12. Such units are held segregated in Zone F as awaiting disposition and remain excluded from available stock for replenishment and picking until approved.

4. Rework is proposed for goods that can be made saleable by defined work in Zone F value-added packing: re-cartoning, relabelling, re-wrapping or rebuild of the pallet within the 1,000 kg pallet limit. Units needing work beyond that definition, with unknown contents, broken hazard seals or temperature failure, are proposed as scrap, not rework.

5. Scrap is proposed for damaged, soiled, leaking, contaminated, expired or otherwise non-conforming goods, and for any unit where identity, batch or safety cannot be verified. Proposed scrap is transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found, flagged in the WMS, and physically segregated from restock and rework candidates.

6. The final disposition of inspected returns is approved only by the shift supervisor in charge. The supervisor reviews the proposal, evidence, counts and quarantine status, orders a second count by stock controllers where quantity or system balance is affected, and records approve or amend by name, date and shift. No adjustment is ever posted without that second count.

7. Value control applies to every scrap decision that writes off stock. The shift supervisor approves write-offs up to and including 500 EUR under PR-09. Any write-off above 500 EUR is approved only by the warehouse manager after quarantine, inspection and documentation. No damaged goods leave quarantine without that recorded approval.

8. Chilled and hazmat returns follow special disposition routes. Chilled units return to Zone E only when the supervisor confirms cold-chain integrity; otherwise they are scrapped via quarantine. Hazardous packed returns go only to the ventilated 60 m2 hazmat cage within its 4,000 kg limit, equivalent to 4 full-weight pallets, or to quarantine under PR-13, and are never restocked to general storage.

9. Approved restock is booked back to available stock by WMS task only. The task states destination — Zone B, Zone E or Zone C via replenishment — and staff move stock between zones only on that task, scan-confirmed at location. Approved rework is completed, re-inspected unit by unit, and only then presented again for restock or scrap decision.

10. The disposition is closed in the WMS when all units of the return are accounted for as restocked, reworked and released, or scrapped with approval, with documents, counts and quarantine records agreeing. Incomplete decisions, held chilled or hazmat units, pending write-offs above 500 EUR and scanner faults are handed over by name under PR-15, with vests and class S3 footwear worn and 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones observed.

title: Quarantine and Write-offs
text:
1. All damaged, suspect or non-conforming goods are quarantined in Zone F services and control under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Quarantine is held only in Zone F and never in Zone A receiving, Zone B bulk storage, Zone C picking, Zone D dispatch or Zone E cold zone.

2. Transfer to quarantine takes place the same day the damage is found. Inbound damage found in Zone A, picking damage found in Zone C, count differences, returns inspection failures, temperature-suspect chilled goods and leaking hazmat packs are all moved to quarantine without delay on a WMS task.

3. Goods enter quarantine with full identity on the 20 handheld WMS scanners. Staff scan the pallet or unit label and quarantine location, record client, product, quantity, batch and expiry where required, inbound or order reference, reason, photographs where required, and flag the stock as quarantine with zero availability for replenishment and picking.

4. Quarantine stock is physically segregated and labelled by reason — damaged, returns awaiting disposition, temperature-hold or hazmat-hold. Quarantine pallets are stable, within footprint and within the 1,000 kg per pallet limit, kept clear of the ventilated 60 m2 hazmat cage, packing benches, wrappers and 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers.

5. No quarantine pallet is moved, reworked, restocked or scrapped without a recorded decision. Returns staff or stock controllers prepare the facts, second count and value, propose restock, rework or scrap, and the authorised approver records the decision in the WMS before any adjustment is posted.

6. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Every quarantine quantity is recounted by a different person, normally the second stock controller or the shift supervisor in charge, and both counts are recorded by name, date and shift before a correction or write-off is proposed.

7. Write-offs are approved strictly by value at the fixed threshold of 500 EUR. The shift supervisor in charge approves damaged-goods write-offs up to and including 500 EUR. Any write-off above 500 EUR is approved only by the warehouse manager after quarantine, inspection and documentation.

8. No damaged goods leave quarantine without that recorded approval. Approved restock returns to available stock only by WMS put-away task to Zone B, Zone E where +2 °C to +8 °C integrity is confirmed under PR-12, or via replenishment to Zone C. Approved rework is completed in Zone F value-added packing and re-inspected unit by unit.

9. Approved scrap is disposed of as directed, with WMS scrap posting only after recount and value approval. Hazardous scrap remains under PR-13, held within the 4,000 kg cage limit equivalent to 4 full-weight pallets or in segregated quarantine, and is never mixed with general waste, baler output or general storage.

10. Quarantine is closed daily and handed over under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Open quarantine quantities, pending second counts, pending approvals above 500 EUR and scanner faults are recorded by name for the next shift, with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn and 10 km/h inside and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones observed.

title: Fleet and Authorisation
text:
1. The internal transport fleet is all electric and is operated only inside the fenced site under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. No diesel or gas-powered truck is used inside the 6,000 m2 hall. The fleet consists of 6 counterbalance forklifts, 4 reach trucks, 8 electric pallet jacks and 12 hand pallet jacks.

2. The 6 counterbalance forklifts are rated at 2.5 t and carry out general work across Zones A to F. This includes unloading in Zone A, transport to the ends of the Zone B rack aisles, support to replenishment and transfer to Zone D, and loading at docks 1-8. Each pallet handled respects the site limit of 1,000 kg including load.

3. The 4 reach trucks are rated at 1.6 t and work the high bays in Zone B bulk storage with its 2,400 pallet positions. They are the only trucks permitted to place and retrieve pallets at height within the 10 m clear height. Counterbalance forklifts deliver to and collect from the aisle ends but do not work inside the high bays.

4. The 8 electric pallet jacks and 12 hand pallet jacks handle small and short moves. Electric pallet jacks are used for replenishment top-ups, packing support and Zone D staging assistance. Hand pallet jacks are used for light positioning, returns moves in Zone F and picker support in Zone C.

5. Ancillary equipment is not part of the driven fleet but is rostered with it. Dispatch operates 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers and 1 cardboard baler, all 8 dock doors have their own leveller operated only by trained staff, and the teams share 20 handheld WMS scanners for all put-away, replenishment, picking and count tasks.

6. The rule for all powered trucks is fixed: no licence, no truck. Counterbalance forklifts, reach trucks and electric pallet jacks are driven only by persons holding the required licence and a current site authorisation. Hand pallet jacks are used only by trained staff assigned to the task by the shift supervisor in charge.

7. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators. No shift supervisor, dispatcher, stock controller, maintenance technician or operator grants, extends or renews driving permission. Authorisation is recorded by name, date, truck types permitted and licence evidence, and is reviewed before any roster change.

8. Authorisation is type-specific and role-bound. The establishment provides 8 forklift operator posts covering counterbalance, reach and electric pallet jack work as authorised per person. Inbound operators, pickers, returns and packing staff, dispatchers and floaters do not drive powered trucks unless they hold a separate manager authorisation as an operator.

9. Every truck is used only after its documented check before first use each day. The check is recorded by truck identity, date and name, defects are reported at once to the shift supervisor and the maintenance technician, and any truck found unsafe is tagged out and not used until repaired and logged.

10. Authorisation is withdrawn on breach or doubt. Expired licence, missed daily check, unsafe driving, aisle or pedestrian breach, overload above 1,000 kg per pallet or bay overload above 2,700 kg, or any damage stops driving immediately. The shift supervisor removes the person from driving, secures the truck, and refers the case to the warehouse manager for decision and handover under PR-15.

title: Daily Checks and Maintenance
text:
1. Every powered truck receives a documented check before its first use each day under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. The check applies to the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t, and the 8 electric pallet jacks. The 12 hand pallet jacks are visually checked before first use for forks, wheels, handle and hydraulics.

2. The check is carried out by the authorised operator assigned to the truck for that shift. The operator uses the daily check sheet by truck identity, confirms licence and site authorisation remain current, and records truck number, date, shift, time and name. An unchecked truck is not started, moved or used for put-away, replenishment, transfer or loading.

3. Each check covers condition and function before load is taken. The operator inspects forks, carriage, chains, hoses and mast for damage, leaks and wear, wheels and tyres for cuts and fixings, overhead guard, seat belt, seat switch, lights, beacon, horn, reverse alarm and display, brakes, steering and hydraulics, and battery charge, connector, cable and electrolyte indication on electric trucks.

4. Reach trucks receive additional high-bay checks for the 10 m clear height work in Zone B. The operator verifies reach extension and retraction, tilt and side-shift, height indicator and load backrest, and capacity plate legibility at 1.6 t. Any fault in lift, reach or height control stops high-bay work until repaired.

5. Any defect found during the check is reported at once to the shift supervisor in charge and to the maintenance technician. The truck is tagged out, keys removed, and the defect recorded with truck identity and description. The supervisor reassigns only a checked truck, and no other operator clears the tag.

6. The maintenance technician — 1 post — owns all repairs to trucks, racking and dock equipment. This includes the forklift and reach-truck fleet, electric and hand pallet jacks, dock levellers at all 8 doors, racking in Zone B, and hardware faults on the 20 handheld WMS scanners. No repair is carried out by unauthorised staff.

7. Every repair is logged by the maintenance technician with date, truck or equipment identity, fault description, parts used, work done, downtime and release signature. The log is kept with the daily check sheets, reviewed by the shift supervisor and the warehouse manager, and handed over by name under PR-15 where work is incomplete.

8. A truck returns to service only after the technician records it as repaired and safe. The next operator carries out a fresh documented check before first use, confirming the repair, and reports any recurrence immediately. Unsafe trucks remain tagged out in a marked area clear of 4.0 m main aisles, 3.0 m rack aisles and 1.2 m walkways.

9. Batteries and charging follow fixed discipline. Electric trucks are charged only in the marked charging area with ventilation and barriers, cables kept clear of pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers, and battery handling by trained staff only. Low-charge trucks are removed from roster and exchanged, not run to failure during put-away or loading.

10. Check sheets and repair logs are closed daily and retained for inspection. Missing checks, repeated defects, overload damage above 1,000 kg per pallet, bay overload above 2,700 kg, or impact damage to uprights or levellers are reported to the warehouse manager, who withdraws authorisation under the no licence, no truck rule where required and orders correction.

title: Safe Driving Rules
text:
1. All driving runs under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation and PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Only authorised operators drive powered trucks on the no licence, no truck rule, only on a truck with a documented check before its first use that day, and only within their authorised types. Any unsafe condition stops driving at once and is reported to the shift supervisor in charge.

2. Speed limits are fixed and enforced on every shift. Inside the 6,000 m2 hall the limit is 10 km/h. In the fenced yard of 3,500 m2 the limit is 15 km/h. Wherever people and trucks meet — marked pedestrian zones, crossings, dock ramps at doors 1-8, and the Zone C pick faces — the limit is 5 km/h. The supervisor stops and reports any speeding.

3. Rated capacities are never exceeded. The 6 counterbalance forklifts are rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks at 1.6 t, and every pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg. The operator reads the capacity plate for load weight and lift height, lowers the load if in doubt, and refuses any overweight, unstable or damaged pallet for quarantine in Zone F the same day.

4. Loads are carried low, stable and within footprint. Forks are fully under the pallet, the mast is tilted back for travel, the load travels at 150-200 mm above the floor, and the operator keeps clear forward vision or drives in reverse with look-back where the load blocks sight. Double-stacking, overhang and dragging pallets are forbidden.

5. Aisle discipline is binding. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide for two-way travel and passing, rack storage aisles in Zone B are 3.0 m wide and kept fully clear for reach-truck work. Operators keep right, signal at blind corners, stop at aisle intersections, and never park, stage or block emergency exits, fire equipment, levellers or Zone E and Zone F doors.

6. Pedestrians have absolute priority. The 1.2 m walkways physically separated by yellow barriers are used by all staff on foot, and trucks never enter, cross unannounced or overhang them. At crossings and shared areas the operator slows to 5 km/h, stops, makes eye contact, sounds the horn, and gives way to inbound operators, pickers, stock controllers and escorted visitors.

7. Seat belts are worn whenever the truck is moving. The operator wears the belt, keeps hands, feet and high-visibility vest inside the overhead guard, and uses lights, beacon, horn and reverse alarm at all times. No passenger is carried, no person stands on forks, and no truck moves with an unbelted operator or raised load in travel mode.

8. Reach-truck work at height follows high-bay discipline within the 10 m clear height. Only the 4 reach trucks work inside the high bays in Zone B, placing at most 2,700 kg per rack bay, checking uprights and beams before placement, and never placing to a damaged, red-tagged or suspended bay. Counterbalance trucks deliver to aisle ends and stay clear of the high-bay envelope.

9. Dock, ramp and yard moves are controlled. The operator serves only the assigned door — 1-4 inbound, 5-8 outbound — with the truck braked and secured and the leveller placed by trained staff, keeps 5 km/h on ramps, never approaches an open edge without a docked trailer, and in the yard keeps to marked lanes, yields to road trucks and keeps clear of the marked driver waiting area.

10. Any impact, overload, near miss or pedestrian breach stops work in that aisle or bay. The operator secures the truck, reports to the shift supervisor, and the bay or area stays closed until inspected, with rack damage logged by the maintenance technician and the incident reviewed before close. Driving resumes only after clearance, recorded by name under PR-15 with vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Aisles and Walkways
text:
1. All internal movement runs on a fixed network of separated walkways and aisles under PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Pedestrians use only the marked walkways, trucks use only the marked aisles, and the two systems cross only at signed crossings. Walking in transport aisles and driving in or across walkways are forbidden.

2. Pedestrian walkways inside the 6,000 m2 hall are 1.2 m wide, marked in full length and physically separated by yellow barriers. They connect the office annex, Zone A to Zone F work areas, crossings, dock interfaces and the emergency exits, and lead to the assembly point by the north fence in an evacuation.

3. Yellow barriers are the separation standard and are binding. Barriers are continuous along walkways bordering main transport aisles, rack aisles and dock approaches, with gaps only at designated crossings and work access points. Missing, loose or displaced barriers are reported at once to the shift supervisor in charge and the maintenance technician.

4. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide and serve two-way electric truck movement between Zones A, B, C, D and F. They are kept fully clear for travel and passing at all times. Staging, put-away, replenishment or dispatch parking in the 4.0 m profile, including single-pallet staging, is forbidden.

5. Rack storage aisles in Zone B bulk storage are 3.0 m wide and are reserved for reach-truck work in the high bays within the 10 m clear height. Counterbalance forklifts deliver to and collect from the aisle ends and do not enter the high-bay envelope. The 3.0 m profile is kept fully clear and no pallet, cage or jack is left in it.

6. Dock approaches, crossings and zone interfaces follow the same discipline. Approaches to doors 1-8 at 1.2 m dock height, leveller swing areas, Zone E cold-zone doors and the Zone F hazmat-cage door are marked keep-clear and never used for staging. Pallet overhang into any aisle, walkway or crossing is treated as a breach.

7. Safety and access keep-clears are absolute. Emergency exits, fire equipment, alarm call points, electrical panels, refrigeration plant, ventilation intakes and first-aid points are kept unobstructed with floor markings respected. Aisles, walkways and crossings in front of them are never blocked, even briefly.

8. Floor markings define the layout and are maintained as equipment. Walkway edges, 4.0 m and 3.0 m aisle edges, block-stack boxes, Zone D staging by door and load, quarantine areas and pedestrian crossings are marked and kept legible. Faded, damaged or confusing markings are reported for re-marking and logged by the maintenance technician.

9. The shift supervisor in charge owns aisle and walkway discipline on the shift. Operators keep right, stop at intersections, give way to pedestrians at crossings at 5 km/h, and secure any load that sheds wrapping or debris. Any blockage, overhang, spill or barrier damage stops movement in that aisle or crossing until cleared.

10. Aisles and walkways are checked daily by the supervisor and verified in the monthly racking inspection and quarterly evacuation drill. Findings — encroachment, overheight block stacks above 3 high or 4.0 m, bay overload above 2,700 kg, barrier or marking defects — are recorded by name, repaired and logged, and unfinished items are handed over under PR-15 with vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Speed Limits
text:
1. Speed limits are fixed for the whole site under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation and PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Inside the 6,000 m2 hall the limit is 10 km/h. In the fenced yard of 3,500 m2 the limit is 15 km/h. Wherever people and trucks meet the limit is 5 km/h. The limits apply on every shift and during any approved Saturday morning overtime.

2. The 10 km/h inside limit applies to all electric trucks in the hall — the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t, and the 8 electric pallet jacks. It covers all movement in Zones A to F, on main transport aisles of 4.0 m, in rack storage aisles of 3.0 m, and on all cross-aisles and zone interfaces.

3. The 15 km/h yard limit applies to all warehouse trucks leaving the hall and to all road vehicles in the yard. Contracted curtain-side trailers, the delivery van and any carrier vehicle keep to marked traffic lanes at 15 km/h, follow dispatcher routing to doors 1-8 at 1.2 m dock height, and never cut across waiting or manoeuvring areas.

4. The 5 km/h limit applies wherever people and trucks meet. This means all marked pedestrian zones, the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers and their crossings, the Zone C pick faces, packing and staging interfaces, and all dock ramps and leveller areas at doors 1-8. At these points trucks slow to walking pace and give way.

5. At pedestrian crossings and shared areas 5 km/h means stop and give way. The operator slows before the crossing, stops, makes eye contact with pedestrians, sounds the horn, and proceeds only when the crossing is clear. Pedestrians on walkways and at crossings have absolute priority and trucks never enter or overhang the 1.2 m profile.

6. At the docks 5 km/h is mandatory on ramps, leveller swing areas and dock approaches. Operators serve only the assigned door — doors 1-4 inbound, doors 5-8 outbound — with the trailer braked and secured and the leveller placed by trained staff, keep 5 km/h on the ramp, and never approach an open edge without a docked trailer.

7. Speed is matched to load and visibility as well as to the sign. Operators reduce below the posted limit with full-weight 1,000 kg pallets, at blind corners, aisle intersections, Zone E and Zone F doors, the hazmat-cage keep-clear, and wherever wrapping, racking or staged pallets in Zone D restrict sight. Loads travel low at 150-200 mm with clear vision or look-back driving.

8. Limits are signed and enforced on the floor. Signs at hall portals, yard entries, crossings and dock ramps state 10, 15 and 5 km/h, floor markings reinforce the zones, and the shift supervisor in charge stops and records any speeding, tailgating or failure to give way. Road drivers who speed are reported to the dispatcher and refused dock access until briefed.

9. Any speeding, near miss, impact or pedestrian breach stops work in that aisle, crossing or dock. The operator or driver secures the vehicle, reports to the shift supervisor, and the area stays closed until inspected, with rack, leveller or barrier damage logged by the maintenance technician. Driving resumes only after clearance and repeat briefing.

10. Speed discipline is checked daily by the supervisor and reviewed in incident reports, monthly racking inspections and the quarterly evacuation drill. Findings — repeated speeding, obscured signs, faded markings or barrier defects — are recorded by name, corrected and logged, and unfinished items are handed over under PR-15, with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: PPE and Pedestrians
text:
1. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor, with no exceptions. The rule covers all Zones A to F, all aisles, dock interfaces and the yard interface, on both shifts 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00 and during any approved Saturday morning overtime.

2. No person enters or remains on the floor without correct PPE in serviceable condition. Vests are worn fastened and visible at all times, footwear is laced and intact to S3 standard, and damaged, missing or non-compliant PPE stops work until replaced. Visitors and contractors follow the same rule and do not pass the office annex without vest and footwear.

3. Forklift operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving, in addition to vest and footwear. The belt is fastened before travel on the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t and the 8 electric pallet jacks where fitted, and remains fastened until the truck is fully stopped and secured.

4. All work on foot runs under PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Pedestrians use only the marked 1.2 m walkways physically separated by yellow barriers, cross truck aisles only at signed crossings, and never walk, stand or wait in main transport aisles of 4.0 m, rack storage aisles of 3.0 m, leveller swing areas or dock approaches.

5. Pedestrians have absolute priority wherever people and trucks meet. At walkway crossings, Zone C pick faces, packing and staging interfaces and dock ramps trucks slow to 5 km/h, stop and give way. Pedestrians make eye contact, wait for the truck to stop, keep to the 1.2 m profile and never step in front of a moving load or raised forks.

6. Pickers, inbound operators, stock controllers and packing staff on foot keep clear of truck envelopes at all times. They do not reach under or between pallets, do not guide loads by hand on forks, keep hands and feet clear of pallet jacks, and give way to authorised operators moving full-weight 1,000 kg pallets low at 150-200 mm.

7. Drivers are pedestrians only in the marked waiting area in the yard. Drivers never enter the 6,000 m2 hall, never use walkways as access to Zones A to F, never operate forklifts, pallet jacks, levellers or WMS scanners, and approach the dock only when called forward by the dispatcher for doors 1-8 at 1.2 m dock height.

8. Behaviour at the dock and in shared areas is controlled. Staff keep behind barriers and keep-clear markings during leveller placement and loading, keep 5 km/h zones fully clear, report loose film, debris or spill immediately, and use lights, horn and eye contact discipline with operators before entering any shared ramp or crossing.

9. The shift supervisor in charge owns PPE and pedestrian discipline on the shift. The supervisor stops any person without vest or S3 footwear, stops any unbelted driving, stops movement on breached barriers or blocked walkways, and records the breach by name for follow-up under PR-10 and PR-11 with referral to the warehouse manager.

10. PPE and pedestrian discipline are checked daily and verified in the monthly racking inspection and quarterly evacuation drill. Findings — missing PPE, unbelted driving, walking in truck aisles, truck overhang of walkways, barrier or marking defects — are recorded by name, corrected and logged by the maintenance technician, and handed over under PR-15 until closed.

title: Evacuation and Drills
text:
1. All evacuation and drill discipline runs under PR-14 Emergency evacuation. The rule is fixed: on alarm everyone leaves the building by the nearest safe exit, assembles at the assembly point by the north fence, completes roll call, and no one re-enters the building until roll call is complete and re-entry is authorised.

2. The shift supervisor in charge owns evacuation on the shift. On alarm or order to evacuate the supervisor stops all work in Zones A to F, stops put-away, replenishment, picking, packing, staging and loading, orders trucks secured where safe, and directs staff, drivers at the docks and escorted visitors to the walkways and exits.

3. Escape routes are the marked 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers continued to signed emergency exits, kept unobstructed at all times. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m and rack aisles of 3.0 m are not escape routes on foot unless directed, and no pallet, jack, wrapper film or baler output is ever placed across a walkway, crossing, exit or fire-equipment approach.

4. On evacuation all staff leave immediately without collecting goods, scanners or paperwork. Forklift operators lower forks to 150-200 mm, stop the truck clear of aisles and exits where safe, switch off, and leave keys in place. Leveller areas at doors 1-8 are left clear and dock work stops with trailers left braked and secured.

5. Drivers in the marked waiting area in the yard and any driver at a dock leave the dock approach and move direct to the assembly point by the north fence. Drivers do not enter the hall to search for warehouse staff, do not move road vehicles in the yard during evacuation, and remain under direction of the supervisor and dispatcher.

6. The assembly point by the north fence is the only roll-call point for both shifts, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, and for any approved Saturday morning overtime. Staff assemble by team — inbound, picking, forklift operators, stock controllers, returns and packing, maintenance, dispatch — so the supervisor can check names against the shift roster and handover list.

7. Roll call is completed before anyone re-enters the building. The shift supervisor calls the roster, records present, missing and injured by name, re-checks Zone E cold-zone and Zone F hazmat-cage attendance separately, and reports the result to the warehouse manager. Search or re-entry for missing persons is ordered only by the supervisor with emergency services.

8. An evacuation drill is run every quarter under PR-14. The drill uses the same alarm, routes and north-fence assembly point as a real evacuation, includes both shift patterns in rotation, and tests walkway discipline, dock stop, truck securing, driver control in the yard, and roll call before authorised re-entry.

9. Each drill is recorded by date, shift, time to clear the 6,000 m2 hall, time to complete roll call, defects found and names of participants. Barrier, marking, exit, alarm and lighting defects are logged by the maintenance technician for repair. The shift supervisor reviews the report and the warehouse manager orders correction where the brief requires it.

10. Re-entry after alarm or drill is controlled. The shift supervisor confirms the building is released by the manager or emergency services, confirms roll call is complete with all persons accounted for, and only then authorises return by walkways to Zones A to F. Unfinished work, suspended WMS tasks and isolated bays are handed over by name under PR-15 before restart.

title: Incident Response
text:
1. Every incident on site — injury, near miss, vehicle impact, rack or building damage, spill or leak, temperature alarm, fire alarm, stock discrepancy or pedestrian breach — is met with immediate response on the floor under PR-14 Emergency evacuation, PR-10, PR-11, PR-12 and PR-13 as applicable. Work in the affected aisle, bay, zone or dock stops until the area is made safe.

2. The shift supervisor in charge leads incident response on the shift. The supervisor stops the operation, secures the area with barriers or tape, directs floor staff and drivers, protects pedestrians on the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers, and takes charge until handover to the next supervisor or escalation to the warehouse manager.

3. People are protected first. Injured persons receive first aid, emergency services are called where needed, and the Zone E cold zone and Zone F hazmat cage are separately checked for persons present. No one re-enters an evacuated or secured area, and roll call at the assembly point by the north fence is completed before re-entry where evacuation applies.

4. Trucks, plant and stock are made safe without creating further risk. Operators lower forks to 150-200 mm, stop clear of 4.0 m main aisles, 3.0 m rack aisles and exits, switch off and leave docked trailers braked and secured at doors 1-8. Leaking hazmat is left unopened, chilled goods are kept at +2 °C to +8 °C where possible, and damaged stock is flagged for quarantine in Zone F the same day.

5. The supervisor informs the warehouse manager without delay on any injury, evacuation, spill, temperature excursion, rack collapse risk, dock damage or loss above 500 EUR. Floor staff report to the supervisor in charge, and dispatchers, stock controllers and the maintenance technician escalate through the supervisor unless immediate escalation to the manager is required.

6. Every incident is reported the same shift it happens. The person involved or discovering it tells the supervisor at once, and the supervisor ensures an incident report is opened with date, time, shift, zone and door, names, truck or equipment identity, description, photographs where required, and immediate action taken on the 20 handheld WMS scanners and paper log as applicable.

7. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report before close or escalation. The review checks facts, second counts where stock is affected, quarantine moves, barrier, rack or leveller damage for the maintenance technician to log and repair, and re-briefing on speed limits of 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas, PPE and no licence, no truck discipline.

8. Follow-up actions are assigned by name and tracked to closure. Damaged goods remain in quarantine in Zone F with no adjustment posted without a second count; write-offs up to and including 500 EUR are approved by the supervisor and above 500 EUR only by the warehouse manager; rack bays above 2,700 kg, block stacks above 3 high or 4.0 m, and pallets above 1,000 kg are stopped from use until cleared.

9. Drivers and visitors are controlled during any incident. Drivers remain in the marked waiting area in the yard, do not enter the hall or move road vehicles unless directed, and contact the floor only at the dock or via the dispatcher. Unauthorised presence in Zones A to F is reported and recorded.

10. Open incidents, isolated bays, suspended WMS tasks and pending repairs are handed over by name under PR-15 End-of-shift handover and reviewed by the warehouse manager. The manager orders correction to operation or manual where the owner's brief requires it, and the supervisor confirms closure only when facts, counts, approvals and repairs agree with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Handover and Shifts
text:
1. Every shift ends with a formal handover under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. The outgoing shift supervisor in charge hands over in person to the incoming supervisor, covering the morning shift 06:00-14:00 and the afternoon shift 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday, plus any approved Saturday morning overtime in peak season.

2. Handover is recorded by name, date and shift. The record states supervisors on duty, floor staffing including floaters deployed, doors and slots handled at doors 1-4 inbound and doors 5-8 outbound, and any absence or roster change. Unrecorded verbal handover is not permitted.

3. Operational status is handed over zone by zone. Zone A arrivals cleared or held for paperwork, put-away to Zone B, E or F outstanding, Zone C faces replenished or needing top-up, Zone D staging by door and load, Zone E temperature and alarms, and Zone F returns, quarantine and the hazmat cage quantity against its 4,000 kg limit are all stated with WMS references.

4. Unfinished WMS work is carried by name. Open put-away, replenishment, picking, packing, staging and count tasks on the 20 handheld scanners, suspended locations, isolated rack bays, blocked doors and tagged-out trucks are listed with owner and next action. No task is left without an owner.

5. Controls due each shift are confirmed as done or carried forward. The manual temperature verification in Zone E between +2 °C and +8 °C, the documented check of every truck before its first use that day, daily cycle counts on the rotating schedule, and quarantine moves the same day damage is found are checked off by the outgoing supervisor.

6. Incidents, defects and breaches are handed over openly. Injuries, near misses, impacts, spills, temperature excursions, speed or PPE breaches, barrier, racking or leveller damage, and every incident report opened are stated with immediate action taken and follow-up assigned for the maintenance technician to log and repair.

7. Overtime is exceptional and centrally controlled. Only the warehouse manager approves overtime, including Saturday morning overtime in peak season. No shift supervisor, dispatcher or operator authorises additional hours, and the handover records approved hours worked, hours carried to the next shift, and any request awaiting manager approval.

8. The incoming shift supervisor starts the next shift from the handover. The supervisor confirms receipt by signature, briefs floor staff at shift start — inbound operators, pickers, forklift operators, stock controllers, returns and packing staff, dispatchers and floaters — allocates tasks, reassigns only checked trucks to authorised operators, and re-sequences replenishment before picking starts.

9. Communication discipline applies throughout. Staff report to the supervisor in charge, dispatchers retain dock scheduling and load release, stock controllers retain second counts with no adjustment posted without a second count, and escalation to the warehouse manager follows the fixed line unless immediate escalation is required.

10. The warehouse manager reviews handover records, count accuracy, incident reviews and inspection logs. Where the manual differs from the owner's brief on how the site is actually run, the brief prevails and the manual is corrected. High-visibility vests and class S3 footwear are worn throughout, with 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas observed on every shift.

title: Forklift Operating Rules
text:
1. All driving of materials-handling equipment on site runs under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. Only trained and authorised persons drive powered trucks, only on a truck with a documented check for that day, and only within their authorisation. Any unsafe truck, load or aisle condition stops driving at once.

2. The fleet is all electric. It consists of 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t for general work, 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t for the high bays in Zone B, 8 electric pallet jacks for small moves and 12 hand pallet jacks for light positioning. No diesel or gas-powered truck is used inside the hall.

3. No licence, no truck. Counterbalance forklifts, reach trucks and electric pallet jacks are driven only by persons holding the required licence and a current site authorisation. Hand pallet jacks are used only by trained staff assigned to the task by the shift supervisor in charge.

4. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators. No shift supervisor, dispatcher, stock controller or operator grants driving permission. Authorisation is recorded by name, truck types permitted and licence evidence, and is type-specific: reach trucks in the high bays are driven only by operators expressly authorised for them.

5. Every powered truck receives a documented check before its first use each day. The assigned operator checks forks, mast, chains, brakes, steering, hydraulics, wheels, lights, beacon, horn, seat belt and battery, and records truck identity, date, shift and name. An unchecked or defective truck is tagged out and not used.

6. Speed limits are fixed and enforced. The limit is 10 km/h inside the building, 15 km/h in the yard, and 5 km/h wherever people and trucks meet — marked pedestrian zones, the 1.2 m walkways and their crossings, the Zone C pick faces, and dock ramps and leveller areas. Pedestrians have absolute priority at 5 km/h points.

7. Seat belts are worn whenever the truck is moving. The operator fastens the belt before travel, keeps body and high-visibility vest inside the overhead guard, and keeps the belt fastened until the truck is fully stopped and secured. No passenger is carried and no truck moves with an unbelted operator.

8. Rated capacities are never exceeded. Every pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg. The operator reads the capacity plate for weight and lift height, carries the load low at 150-200 mm with masts tilted back, and refuses overweight, unstable or damaged pallets. Such pallets go to quarantine in Zone F the same day.

9. Aisle and dock discipline is binding. Operators use main transport aisles of 4.0 m for travel, keep 3.0 m rack aisles fully clear for reach-truck work, keep right, signal at blind corners and stop at intersections. At docks they serve only the assigned door with the trailer braked and secured, keep 5 km/h on ramps, and never approach an open edge without a docked trailer.

10. Any impact, overload, near miss or pedestrian breach stops work in that aisle, bay or dock. The operator secures the truck, reports at once to the shift supervisor in charge, and the area stays closed until inspected. Defects and damage are logged by the maintenance technician, and driving resumes only after clearance is recorded.

title: Pedestrian Walkways and Crossings
text:
1. All movement on foot inside the site runs under PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Pedestrians use only marked walkways, trucks use only marked aisles, and the two systems meet only at signed crossings. Walking in transport aisles and driving in walkways are forbidden.

2. Pedestrian walkways inside the 6,000 m2 hall are 1.2 m wide, marked in full length and physically separated by yellow barriers. They connect the office annex, Zones A to F work areas, crossings, dock interfaces and emergency exits, and lead to the assembly point by the north fence.

3. Yellow barriers are the separation standard and are binding. Barriers are continuous along walkways beside main transport aisles, rack aisles and dock approaches, with gaps only at designated crossings and work access points. Missing, loose or displaced barriers are reported at once to the shift supervisor in charge.

4. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide for two-way electric truck movement. Rack storage aisles in Zone B are 3.0 m wide for reach-truck work in the high bays. Pedestrians never walk, stand or wait in either aisle type, and never take shortcuts across aisles outside a marked crossing.

5. Crossings are signed, marked and kept fully clear. Trucks slow to 5 km/h before the crossing, stop, make eye contact, sound the horn and give way. Pedestrians wait at the barrier edge, check the aisle is clear, keep to the marked profile, and never step in front of a moving load or raised forks.

6. The 5 km/h rule applies wherever people and trucks meet — marked pedestrian zones, walkways and crossings, the Zone C pick faces, packing and staging interfaces, and dock ramps and leveller areas at doors 1-8. At these points trucks travel at walking pace and pedestrians have absolute priority.

7. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor, with no exceptions. No person enters or remains on walkways, in Zones A to F, or at the dock interface without correct PPE in serviceable condition, fastened and visible at all times.

8. Drivers are pedestrians only in the marked waiting area in the yard. Drivers never enter the hall, never use the 1.2 m walkways to access Zones A to F, never cross the dock leveller areas on foot without being called forward, and never operate forklifts, pallet jacks, levellers or WMS scanners.

9. Walkways, crossings, exits and keep-clears are never blocked. No pallet, jack, wrapper film, baler output or staged load is placed across a walkway, crossing, emergency exit, fire-equipment approach, Zone E door or Zone F hazmat-cage door. Pallet overhang into any walkway or crossing is treated as a breach.

10. The shift supervisor in charge owns walkway and crossing discipline on the shift. The supervisor stops any walking in truck aisles, any truck overhang or failure to give way, and any blocked walkway or damaged barrier, records the breach by name, and hands unfinished corrections over under PR-15. Speed limits of 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas are enforced.

title: Yard and Dock Safety
text:
1. All vehicle movement and dock work in the yard runs under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse, with inbound under PR-01 and outbound under PR-06. The fenced yard of 3,500 m2 is a controlled traffic area, and discipline at doors, ramps and waiting areas is enforced by the shift supervisor in charge on every shift.

2. Access to the yard is by booking only. The dispatcher books transport, assigns every carrier a specific door and a fixed time slot, and records carrier, trailer, client and pallet count. Only scheduled carriers with an assigned door and slot are admitted, and early, late or unbooked trucks wait as directed without occupying a dock.

3. Doors 1-4 are inbound only serving Zone A receiving, and doors 5-8 are outbound only serving Zone D dispatch. The separation is absolute and no truck is directed to, or worked at, a door in the reverse direction. The dispatcher coordinates the sequence across all 8 doors to avoid congestion and dock conflicts.

4. All dock doors are at 1.2 m dock height and each has its own dock leveller. Levellers are operated only by trained warehouse staff assigned by the shift supervisor. Drivers never operate levellers, forklifts, pallet jacks or WMS scanners, and never enter the hall beyond the dock edge.

5. Road vehicles keep to marked traffic lanes, manoeuvring boxes and stop lines in the yard. Reversing to the assigned door is guided where required, with the truck centred, braked and secured before the leveller is placed. No trailer is worked until braked and secured, and no forklift approaches an open dock edge without a docked trailer in place.

6. Speed limits in the yard are fixed and enforced. The limit is 15 km/h on marked traffic lanes and manoeuvring areas, and 5 km/h wherever people and trucks meet — marked pedestrian zones, walkway crossings, dock ramps, leveller swing areas and dock approaches. Road drivers who speed are stopped, reported to the dispatcher, and refused dock access until re-briefed.

7. Drivers are pedestrians only in the marked waiting area in the yard. On arrival drivers report at the assigned door, present documents, then return to the waiting area until called forward for loading or unloading. Drivers do not enter the 6,000 m2 hall, do not use the 1.2 m internal walkways, and remain clear of forklift movements, leveller areas and pedestrian crossings.

8. Dock approaches, leveller swing areas, pedestrian crossings and keep-clear markings are never blocked. No pallet, jack, wrapper film or staged load is placed on ramps or across yard crossings, and pallet overhang from the dock into the yard lane is treated as a breach. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are mandatory for everyone at the dock and yard interface, with no exceptions.

9. Forklift work between hall and dock follows aisle and ramp discipline. Operators use main transport aisles of 4.0 m inside, keep 5 km/h on ramps and leveller areas, carry loads low at 150-200 mm with clear vision, keep right and stop at blind corners and intersections. Seat belts are worn whenever the truck is moving, and pedestrians have absolute priority at all 5 km/h points.

10. Any near miss, impact, barrier or leveller damage, unsecured trailer, unauthorised presence or blocked ramp stops work at that door. The operator or driver secures the vehicle, reports at once to the shift supervisor in charge, and the door stays closed until inspected. Damage is logged by the maintenance technician, and work and unfinished corrections are handed over by name under PR-15.

title: Mandatory PPE
text:
1. Personal protective equipment on the warehouse floor is mandatory under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation and PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are required for everyone on the floor, with no exceptions, on every shift.

2. The rule covers the entire 6,000 m2 hall — Zones A to F, all main transport aisles of 4.0 m, rack storage aisles of 3.0 m, the 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers, crossings, and the dock interfaces at doors 1-8. It applies on both shifts, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, and during any approved Saturday morning overtime.

3. No person enters or remains on the floor without correct PPE in serviceable condition. Vests are worn fastened, closed and fully visible over outer clothing at all times. Footwear is worn laced, intact and to S3 standard. Damaged, missing, unfastened or non-compliant PPE stops that person working until replaced.

4. High-visibility vests are worn by all roles: warehouse manager, shift supervisors, forklift operators, inbound operators, pickers, stock controllers, returns and packing staff, maintenance technician, dispatchers and floaters. Torn, faded, heavily soiled or non-reflective vests are treated as missing and are exchanged immediately.

5. Class S3 safety footwear is worn by everyone on the floor, without exception for office staff, visitors or contractors passing beyond the office annex. Trainers, low shoes, sandals or any non-S3 footwear are forbidden on the floor, in the yard interface and at the dock edge. Defective footwear with split uppers, worn soles or failed fastening is replaced before work resumes.

6. Forklift operators wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving, in addition to vest and S3 footwear. The belt is fastened before travel on the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t and the 8 electric pallet jacks where belts are fitted, and remains fastened until the truck is fully stopped and secured.

7. No truck moves with an unbelted operator, no passenger is carried, and no person stands on forks or on a pallet. The operator keeps body, hands, feet and vest inside the overhead guard. An unbelted move is stopped at once as a breach of PR-10, the truck is secured, and the case is reported to the shift supervisor in charge.

8. Drivers and visitors follow the same floor rule. Drivers remain as pedestrians only in the marked waiting area in the yard and do not enter the hall. Where a driver is lawfully at the dock edge or an escorted visitor enters the floor, vest and S3 footwear are mandatory, and entry without them is refused.

9. The shift supervisor in charge owns PPE discipline on the shift. The supervisor stops any person without vest or S3 footwear, stops any unbelted driving, removes the person from the floor or the truck, records the breach by name, and refers repeated or wilful breaches to the warehouse manager. Speed discipline of 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas continues in parallel.

10. PPE is checked daily by the supervisor and handed over by name under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Missing PPE, unbelted driving, defective vests or footwear, and stocks for replacement are recorded with names and corrective action. The warehouse manager reviews the records and orders correction where the owner's brief requires it.

title: Racking and Stacking Limits
text:
1. All storage in Zone B bulk storage runs under PR-02 Put-away to storage and PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. No pallet is placed in racking or in block stack unless its weight, condition and location have been checked. Any overload, damage or unstable load stops put-away to that bay or floor area at once.

2. The governing weight for all storage is 1,000 kg per pallet, load included. No pallet placed in a rack bay or in free block-stacking exceeds this limit. Operators read the pallet identity and refuse any overweight, leaning or damaged pallet, which goes to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found.

3. Each rack bay in the high-bay racking carries at most 2,700 kg in total, including pallets, goods and pallet timber. In practice this means no more than two full-weight pallets per bay. The remaining margin is reserved for weight variation and safe handling, and the bay label is never exceeded.

4. The racking stands within the 10 m clear height of the hall and holds 2,400 pallet positions in the 2,200 m2 bulk store. Only the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t place and retrieve pallets at height. The 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t deliver to and collect from the aisle ends and do not work inside the high bays.

5. Free block-stacking is permitted only in marked floor areas outside the racking. In those areas stacking is limited to 3 pallets high and to 4.0 m total height including pallets and load, whichever is reached first. Any stack that would exceed either limit is split and relocated, never topped up.

6. No rack pallet and no block stack may overhang the aisle, walkway or location footprint. Pallets must be sound, fully wrapped or otherwise secured, evenly loaded and placed squarely within the beams or floor marking. Damaged, leaning, unwrapped or unstable pallets are not put to height or to stack.

7. Aisles, exits and keep-clears around storage are absolute. Main transport aisles of 4.0 m and rack storage aisles of 3.0 m are kept fully clear, as are the 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers, crossings, dock approaches, emergency exits, fire equipment and the Zone E and Zone F doors. No block stack is placed in these profiles.

8. Uprights, beams, bracing, base plates and fixings are checked before placement. The operator confirms beams are level and engaged and the bay shows no impact damage, bending, missing pins or red tag before placing the load. Placement to a damaged, red-tagged or suspended bay is forbidden.

9. All racking receives a documented safety inspection every month. The maintenance technician together with the shift supervisor in charge checks every bay for load, damage and marking, checks block-stack heights and aisle clearances, records results bay by bay, and logs every repair. The warehouse manager reviews the log.

10. Any bay found above 2,700 kg, any block stack above 3 high or 4.0 m, any impact or structural damage, or any encroachment into aisles or walkways is made safe immediately. The shift supervisor stops work in that bay or area, secures it with barriers or tape, orders unloading or rebuilding by an authorised operator, and work resumes only after clearance is recorded under PR-15.

title: Daily Checks and Maintenance
text:
1. Every powered truck receives a documented safety check before its first use each day under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. The rule covers the 6 counterbalance forklifts rated at 2.5 t, the 4 reach trucks rated at 1.6 t and the 8 electric pallet jacks. The 12 hand pallet jacks are visually checked for forks, wheels, handle and hydraulics before first use.

2. The check is carried out by the authorised operator assigned to that truck for the shift. The operator confirms licence and site authorisation are current, works through the daily sheet by truck identity, and records truck number, date, shift, time and name. An unchecked truck is not started, moved or loaded.

3. The check covers the full safe condition of the truck before any pallet up to 1,000 kg is taken. Forks, carriage, chains, hoses and mast, wheels and fixings, overhead guard, seat belt and seat switch, lights, beacon, horn and reverse alarm, brakes, steering and hydraulics, and battery charge, connector and cables on all-electric trucks are inspected and function-tested.

4. Reach trucks for the high bays in Zone B receive additional checks for work within the 10 m clear height. Reach extension and retraction, tilt and side-shift, height indicator, load backrest and legibility of the 1.6 t capacity plate are verified. Any fault in lift, reach or height control stops all high-bay work with that truck.

5. Any defect found is reported at once to the shift supervisor in charge and to the maintenance technician. The truck is tagged out with keys removed, the defect is recorded by truck identity and description, and the supervisor reassigns only a checked truck. No other person clears the tag or returns the truck to use.

6. The maintenance technician, 1 post, owns all repairs to trucks, racking and dock equipment. This includes the forklift and reach-truck fleet, electric and hand pallet jacks, dock levellers at all 8 doors at 1.2 m dock height, and racking in Zone B. No repair is carried out by unauthorised staff.

7. Every repair is logged with date, equipment identity, fault description, parts used, work done, downtime and release signature. The log is kept with the daily check sheets, reviewed by the shift supervisor and the warehouse manager, and unfinished work is handed over by name under PR-15 End-of-shift handover.

8. A truck returns to service only after the technician records it as repaired and safe. The next operator carries out a fresh documented check before first use and reports any recurrence immediately. Tagged-out trucks are parked in a marked area clear of 4.0 m main aisles, 3.0 m rack aisles and 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers.

9. Racking and dock equipment are checked on the same discipline. Operators confirm bay condition, beam engagement and absence of red tags before placing to height, and confirm the leveller and dock edge before serving doors 1-4 inbound and 5-8 outbound. All high-bay racking with 2,400 positions receives a documented safety inspection every month for bay loads to 2,700 kg, damage, markings and aisle clearances.

10. Check sheets, racking logs and repair logs are closed daily and retained for inspection. Missing checks, repeated defects, overload damage, impact to uprights, beams or levellers, or barrier damage stop work in that bay or door until cleared. The shift supervisor enforces the no licence, no truck rule and 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas, with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Working in the Cold Zone
text:
1. Work in Zone E cold zone runs under PR-12 Cold-chain handling. Zone E is a fixed 300 m2 chilled store inside the hall and holds only goods requiring chill. No ambient, hazmat, packing or quarantine stock is held, staged or left in Zone E.

2. The storage condition in Zone E is held between +2 °C and +8 °C at all times. The range applies to every position in the zone on every shift, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00, and during any approved Saturday morning overtime. No chilled product is stored outside Zone E to use spare capacity.

3. Temperature is monitored by fixed alarms plus a manual verification each shift. The shift supervisor in charge ensures the manual check is carried out, with measured value, time, zone, and name recorded. The record is kept with shift documents and handed over under PR-15.

4. Chilled deliveries are flagged by the dispatcher at booking and priority-checked in Zone A for temperature, packaging and condition. They are booked to Zone E only when cold-chain integrity is confirmed, and put away direct to Zone E without delay. Any temperature doubt stops booking for supervisor decision.

5. If the temperature reaches or passes outside +2 °C to +8 °C, or any alarm activates, work with chilled goods stops. The shift supervisor takes charge, secures the zone, checks doors and plant, segregates affected stock in the WMS, informs the warehouse manager, and holds put-away, replenishment, picking and dispatch until clearance is recorded.

6. Door and dwell discipline keeps the condition stable. Zone E doors are kept closed except for immediate put-away, count, replenishment or picking moves. Pallets are not staged in the doorway, in transport aisles or in Zone A longer than needed, and chilled pallets are returned to temperature immediately after scan confirmation.

7. Only authorised operators on checked electric trucks move pallets in Zone E on a WMS task. Each pallet, load included, weighs at most 1,000 kg. Operators observe 10 km/h inside the building and 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps, and keep 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers and Zone E approaches fully clear.

8. High-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear are mandatory in Zone E with no exceptions. Staff minimise time in the cold, keep doors closed between moves, report slippery floors, condensation, ice build-up or faulty lighting at once, and do not remain in the zone when feeling unwell. The supervisor controls rotation on long cold work.

9. Stock in Zone E is counted on the daily rotating schedule with minimal door-open time, and no adjustment is ever posted without a second count. Counters batch locations, keep doors closed except for immediate access, and transfer damaged, leaking, unlabelled or temperature-suspect goods to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found.

10. The maintenance technician owns the refrigeration plant, door seals, alarms and temperature displays and logs every repair. Any fault, alarm failure, door defect or missed manual verification is reported at once to the shift supervisor and the warehouse manager, stops routine chilled put-away until made safe, and is handed over by name under PR-15 until closed.

title: Hazmat Storage Limits
text:
1. All storage of hazardous packed goods on site runs under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. No hazmat is received, moved, stored or dispatched outside this control. Any unsafe packaging, labelling or quantity condition stops intake and put-away at once.

2. The only place where hazmat may be held is the separate ventilated hazmat cage inside Zone F services and control. The cage has a fixed floor area of 60 m2, is physically separated from packing, quarantine and returns inspection, is marked, signed and kept locked except for an authorised move on a WMS task.

3. Hazmat never sits anywhere else in the hall or yard. It is not stored in Zone B bulk storage, Zone C picking, Zone D dispatch or Zone E cold zone, or elsewhere in Zone F. In Zone A it remains only segregated under supervision for document and label checking on arrival, and is then moved by escorted put-away to the cage only.

4. The cage holds never more than 4,000 kg of hazardous goods at a time. The limit applies to the combined weight of goods, packaging and pallets inside the cage at any moment, on both shifts 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, and during any approved Saturday morning overtime. No new booking is released if it would exceed the limit.

5. The governing pallet weight of 1,000 kg, load included, applies in full. At most 4 full-weight pallets may be in the cage at one time. Lighter pallets do not create extra places: the kilogram limit and the 4-pallet equivalent together cap quantity, and the shift supervisor in charge stops intake when either is reached.

6. Deliveries containing hazmat are flagged by the dispatcher at booking with client, product and quantity. In Zone A they are checked against papers and hazard labels without opening the packs, segregated from general goods, and booked only to the cage. Booking is checked against current cage stock in the WMS before any put-away task is issued.

7. If a delivery would exceed 4,000 kg, the excess is not booked for put-away. It remains held segregated under supervision in Zone A or is re-booked by the dispatcher, and is recorded with reason, quantity and name. Returns containing hazmat received in Zone F go only to the cage within the limit or to quarantine, never to general storage.

8. Put-away, removal and counting moves use only authorised forklift operators on trucks with a documented check before first use that day, on a WMS task stating cage location. A second person escorts where PR-13 requires it. Pallets are scan-confirmed at the cage location, stable, within footprint, fully labelled and never double-stacked unless the cage layout expressly permits it.

9. Separation inside and around the cage is mandatory. The cage is kept clear of packing materials, baler output, quarantine pallets and general staging. The keep-clear zone at the cage door for access, ventilation and spill response is never used for staging, and 1.2 m pedestrian walkways behind yellow barriers, 4.0 m main aisles and dock approaches are kept fully clear.

10. Quantity and condition are checked before every move and verified on the daily rotating cycle counts, with no adjustment ever posted without a second count. Any excess, miscount, unlabelled pallet, leak, odour or damaged packaging stops all cage work for assessment by the shift supervisor in charge. Faults in ventilation, lighting or signage are reported to the maintenance technician, logged, and intake stays stopped until clearance is recorded and handed over by name under PR-15, with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear worn throughout.

title: Spills and Damaged Goods
text:
1. All spill, leak and damage response on site runs under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response and PR-09 Damaged-goods handling, with PR-12 Cold-chain handling for chilled goods. Any spill, leak, odour, damaged packaging, unreadable label or unstable pallet stops work at that location at once and is reported to the shift supervisor in charge.

2. The operator or person discovering the spill stops the truck or task safely, leaves the immediate area safe without spreading contamination, warns others, and alerts the supervisor. No clean-up is started with bare hands, no leaking pack is opened, and no further put-away, picking or dispatch of the affected goods takes place until the supervisor has assessed.

3. The shift supervisor takes charge of the area, secures it with barriers or tape, keeps pedestrians on the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers, keeps 4.0 m main aisles and 3.0 m rack aisles clear for access, and ensures ventilation at the Zone F 60 m2 hazmat cage and fresh air in Zone E. The supervisor informs the warehouse manager without delay on any hazmat spill, injury, or loss risk above 500 EUR.

4. Spill clean-up uses only the designated spill equipment for the substance, operated by instructed staff under supervision with high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear worn. Absorbents and contaminated materials are collected, bagged and labelled, never swept into drains, aisles or general waste, and never mixed with cardboard baler output.

5. All damaged, leaking, contaminated, temperature-suspect or non-conforming goods are segregated at once and transferred to quarantine in Zone F the same day they are found. This covers inbound damage in Zone A, picking damage in Zone C, count finds in Zone B and Zone E, cage finds, and returns failures. Quarantine is held only in Zone F, never in Zone B, C, D or E.

6. Goods enter quarantine with full WMS identity on the handheld scanners: client, product, quantity, batch and expiry where required, reference, reason, photographs where required, and quarantine status with zero availability. Pallets respect 1,000 kg, load included, are stable and within footprint, and hazmat quarantine remains segregated under PR-13 within the 4,000 kg cage discipline.

7. No quarantine pallet is moved, reworked, restocked or scrapped without a recorded decision. Stock controllers or returns staff prepare facts and a second count, propose restock, rework or scrap, and the authorised approver records the decision before any adjustment. No adjustment is ever posted without a second count by a different person.

8. Write-offs follow the fixed 500 EUR threshold. The shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to and including 500 EUR and the final disposition of inspected returns. Any write-off above 500 EUR is approved only by the warehouse manager after quarantine, inspection and documentation. No damaged goods leave quarantine without that recorded approval.

9. Zone E and hazmat spills follow special discipline. Chilled spills or temperature excursions hold the +2 °C to +8 °C stock, doors stay closed except for immediate action, and affected units go to quarantine in Zone F the same day. Hazmat leaks, odour or damaged hazard seals stop all cage work, the cage keep-clear and ventilation are kept free, and re-entry is only on supervisor clearance.

10. Every spill and damage is reported the same shift, logged with date, time, zone, names and action taken, and handed over by name under PR-15 End-of-shift handover. The maintenance technician logs repairs to racking, spill and fire equipment, ventilation and alarms, and the shift supervisor reviews every report, enforces 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas, and keeps the bay or door closed until clearance is recorded.

title: Incident Reporting
text:
1. Every injury, near miss, vehicle impact, rack or building damage, spill or leak, temperature or fire alarm, stock discrepancy and pedestrian or speed breach is reported on site. Work in the affected aisle, bay, zone or dock stops until the area is made safe and the report is opened under PR-10, PR-11, PR-12, PR-13 and PR-14 as applicable.

2. The person involved in or discovering the incident tells the shift supervisor in charge at once, in person, on the same shift. Floor staff report to the supervisor, and dispatchers, stock controllers and the maintenance technician escalate through the supervisor unless immediate escalation to the warehouse manager is required for injury or evacuation.

3. The shift supervisor takes charge of the floor, secures the area with barriers or tape, protects pedestrians on the 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers, and ensures first aid and emergency services where needed. The supervisor informs the warehouse manager without delay on any injury, evacuation, spill, temperature excursion, rack collapse risk or loss above 500 EUR.

4. An incident report is opened the same shift the incident happens, before handover. It records date, time, shift, zone and door, names of persons involved and witnesses, truck or equipment identity, description of what happened, photographs where required, and immediate action taken on barriers, trucks and stock.

5. Injuries and near misses are recorded with the same discipline, including first-aid given, time off the floor, and rotation or task change ordered. A near miss with a forklift, reach truck or pallet jack at 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard or 5 km/h at pedestrian zones, crossings and ramps is treated as a driving breach and the operator is stood down pending review.

6. Damage to racking, levellers, barriers, trucks or stock is recorded with location, bay and load detail. Bay loads above 2,700 kg, block stacks above 3 high or 4.0 m, and pallets above 1,000 kg are stated with weights, and damaged stock is flagged in the WMS and moved to quarantine in Zone F the same day it is found.

7. Where stock accuracy is affected, no adjustment is ever posted without a second count. The report notes the first and second counts by name, with location, product, quantity, batch and expiry where required, and quarantine status. Write-offs up to and including 500 EUR await supervisor approval and above 500 EUR await warehouse manager approval.

8. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report before close or escalation. The review checks facts, counts, quarantine moves, spill clean-up, ventilation and alarm condition, PPE with high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear, seat-belt use and no licence, no truck compliance, and orders re-briefing and repair logging by the maintenance technician.

9. Follow-up actions are assigned by name with a due time and tracked to closure. Isolated bays, suspended WMS tasks, tagged-out trucks and closed doors remain closed until clearance is recorded. Unfinished actions, pending approvals and repairs are handed over by name under PR-15 End-of-shift handover to the next supervisor.

10. The warehouse manager reviews shift records, incident reviews and inspection logs. Where the manual differs from the owner's brief on how the site is actually run, the brief prevails and the manual is corrected. Closure is confirmed only when facts, counts, approvals and repairs agree.

title: Evacuation and Re-entry
text:
1. All evacuation and re-entry on site runs under PR-14 Emergency evacuation. On alarm or ordered evacuation everyone leaves the building at once by the nearest safe exit, assembles at the assembly point by the north fence, completes roll call, and no one re-enters the building until roll call is complete and re-entry is authorised.

2. The shift supervisor in charge owns the evacuation on the shift. The supervisor stops all work in Zones A to F, stops put-away, replenishment, picking, packing, staging and loading, orders trucks secured where safe to do so, and directs staff, drivers at the docks and escorted visitors to the walkways and exits.

3. Escape routes are the marked 1.2 m pedestrian walkways physically separated by yellow barriers, continued to signed emergency exits. Walkways, crossings, exits and fire-equipment approaches are kept unobstructed at all times. No pallet, jack, wrapper film or baler output is ever placed across an escape route.

4. Staff leave immediately without collecting goods, scanners, paperwork or personal items from racks or benches. Forklift operators lower forks to 150-200 mm, stop clear of 4.0 m main aisles, 3.0 m rack aisles and exits where safe, switch off, and leave keys in place. Work at doors 1-8 stops with trailers left braked and secured and leveller areas left clear.

5. Drivers in the marked waiting area in the yard and any driver at a dock leave the dock approach and move direct to the assembly point by the north fence. Drivers do not enter the 6,000 m2 hall to search for staff, do not move road vehicles during evacuation, and remain under direction of the supervisor and dispatcher.

6. The assembly point by the north fence is the only roll-call point for both shifts, 06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00, and for any approved Saturday morning overtime. Staff assemble by team — inbound, picking, forklift operators, stock controllers, returns and packing, maintenance and dispatch — so names can be checked against the roster and handover list.

7. Roll call is completed before anyone re-enters the building. The shift supervisor calls the roster, records present, missing and injured by name, checks Zone E cold zone and Zone F hazmat-cage attendance separately, and reports the result to the warehouse manager. Search or re-entry for missing persons is ordered only with emergency services.

8. An evacuation drill is run every quarter under PR-14. The drill uses the same alarm, escape routes and north-fence assembly point as a real evacuation, rotates to cover both shift patterns, and tests walkway discipline, dock stop, truck securing, driver control in the yard, and roll call before authorised re-entry.

9. Each drill and each real evacuation is recorded with date, shift, time to clear the hall, time to complete roll call, defects found and names of participants. Defects to barriers, markings, exits, alarms, lighting and levellers are logged by the maintenance technician for repair. The shift supervisor reviews the report and the warehouse manager orders correction.

10. Re-entry after alarm or drill is controlled. The building is released only by the warehouse manager or emergency services, the supervisor confirms roll call is complete with all persons accounted for, and only then authorises return by walkways to Zones A to F in high-visibility vests and class S3 safety footwear. Suspended WMS tasks, isolated bays and unfinished checks are handed over by name under PR-15 before restart.

title: Safety Roles and Handover
text:
1. Accountability for safety at Harborwick 3PL Ltd. rests with the warehouse manager as owner of the site. The manager is accountable for operations, safety and inventory accuracy across the 6,000 m2 hall and 3,500 m2 yard, owns procedures PR-10 to PR-15, and is the final sign-off for safe operation. Where the manual differs from the owner's brief, the brief prevails.

2. The shift supervisor in charge is responsible for safety and order on the floor on every shift, mornings 06:00-14:00 and afternoons 14:00-22:00, plus any approved Saturday morning overtime. The supervisor allocates tasks, enforces speed limits, aisle discipline, PPE and dock discipline, leads incident response, and hands over formally under PR-15 End-of-shift handover.

3. Only the warehouse manager authorises new forklift operators under the no licence, no truck rule, approves overtime, and signs off the annual wall-to-wall stocktake and any damaged-goods write-off above 500 EUR. No supervisor, dispatcher or operator grants driving permission or overtime.

4. The shift supervisor exercises fixed safety approvals on the shift. The supervisor approves write-offs up to and including 500 EUR, approves the final disposition of inspected returns as restock, rework or scrap, stops any unsafe truck, bay, aisle or door, and reviews every incident report before close or escalation to the warehouse manager.

5. The dispatcher owns dock scheduling and load release for safety at the interface. The dispatcher books transport, assigns doors 1-4 inbound only and 5-8 outbound only with time slots, directs drivers to the marked waiting area, and releases outbound loads only when pallets are wrapped, labelled and staged. No truck is worked without release.

6. Forklift operators, inbound operators, pickers, stock controllers, returns and packing staff, floaters and the maintenance technician work safety within role. Operators drive only authorised types on checked trucks, all staff wear high-visibility vests and class S3 footwear, use 1.2 m walkways behind yellow barriers, observe 10 km/h inside, 15 km/h in the yard and 5 km/h in shared areas, and report defects at once.

7. The maintenance technician, 1 post, owns the safe condition of plant. This covers the 6 counterbalance forklifts at 2.5 t, 4 reach trucks at 1.6 t, pallet jacks, levellers at all 8 doors, racking with 2,400 positions, barriers, alarms and spill equipment. Every repair is logged, and tagged-out trucks and red-tagged bays stay closed until cleared.

8. Every shift ends with a recorded handover by name, date and shift from outgoing to incoming supervisor. Verbal-only handover is forbidden. The record states staffing, doors handled, Zone A to F status, Zone E temperature between +2 °C and +8 °C with manual verification, hazmat cage quantity against 4,000 kg, and quarantine in Zone F.

9. Unfinished safety work is carried by name with owner and next action. Open incident reports, isolated bays above 2,700 kg or block stacks above 3 high or 4.0 m, tagged-out trucks without a daily check, suspended WMS tasks, barrier, leveller or alarm defects, and pending second counts and approvals are listed and remain closed until clearance is recorded.

10. The warehouse manager reviews handover records, incident reviews, cycle-count accuracy, monthly racking inspections and quarterly evacuation drills with roll call at the north fence. Closure is confirmed only when facts, counts, approvals and repairs agree, with unfinished items carried forward under PR-15 until closed.

title: Warehouse Manager
text:
1. The Warehouse Manager is the owner of Harborwick 3PL Ltd. and is accountable for the whole site — day-to-day operations, safety, inventory accuracy and client service across the 6,000 m2 hall and 3,500 m2 fenced yard in Port Sellow. Where day-to-day running is delegated to the shift supervisor in charge, dispatchers or stock controllers, accountability remains with the Warehouse Manager.
